Embodied First Exam

Kangrui Wang1∗§, Qineng Wang1∗§, Changhe Chen1∗§, Pingyue Zhang1∗§, Chi Gui1∗§, Feishi Wang1∗§, Canyu Chen1∗§, Wenli Xiao2§, Xiaoyu Huang3§, Tonghe Zhang2§, Linjie Li4§, Zihan Wang1, Minyeong Kim5, Yiyou Sun3, Mingkai Deng2, Jinyu Hou2, Qi Zhu1, Han Liu1, Eric P. Xing2, Huaxiu Yao6, Zhiwen Fan7, Yuejiang Liu5, Dawn Song3, Pieter Abbeel3, Li Fei-Fei5, Jiajun Wu5, Yuke Zhu8, Guanya Shi2†, Ruohan Zhang1†, Manling Li1†
1Northwestern University 2Carnegie Mellon University 3UC Berkeley 4University of Washington
5Stanford University 6UNC-Chapel Hill 7Texas A&M University 8UT Austin
∗Equal contribution §Core contributor †Equal advising
Abstract

Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives the agent access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution for training purposes. Success rates in this setting serve as an approximate upper bound. On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves a success rate of 34% in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement. To see where agents fail, we label the stage at which failed attempts go wrong and compare failures across agents, settings, and stage categories.

1 Introduction

Robots acquire new skills either by manual programming or by learning from data, as in recent vision-language-action models [11, 69, 10, 122, 110, 38] and world action models [182, 159, 133]. Coding agents powered by large language models suggest a third way. They already complete challenging software engineering tasks in the digital world [64, 102, 104, 73]. What makes these agents promising for robotic engineering is their capabilities to turn instructions into executable code and revise their plans through automated experimentation [84, 141, 151]. Recent early success in agentic robots suggests such a potential paradigm shift, where agents directly control robots [47, 191, 199, 130], write robot programs [62, 32, 101, 167, 145, 48], or train policies [165, 83]. This motivates a systematic assessment of the capability boundary of coding agents:

Existing benchmarks do not yet fully address this question. The capability boundary cannot be established from a focused set of robotics tasks [59, 184, 87, 76, 106, 16], nor from automated programming tasks without imposing physical-world constraints [64, 102, 198, 168, 14, 116]. This requires defining which robotic capabilities to evaluate, measuring how physical-world constraints affect success, and supporting different models and harnesses through task interfaces.

To answer this question, we introduce the Embodied First Exam (EFE), a unified evaluation framework that connects coding agents to simulated robots (), following three principles.

First, include diverse tasks that go beyond pick-and-place. Spatial puzzles test reasoning about spatial constraints, while sim-to-sim engineering tests how agents revise controllers from execution feedback under unfamiliar dynamics. Dynamic tasks test responses to a changing world. Multi-robot interaction and whole-body control test coordination. EFE therefore contains 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots. It combines 26 suites adapted from existing robotics benchmarks with 9 new suites covering these capabilities and safety.

Second, measure how success depends on physical-world constraints. Its tasks should follow the constraints of a real robot as closely as possible. Success with full simulator state and resets does not establish what an agent can achieve through partial observations, with no resets, or while the dynamic world keeps running. We therefore define up to three evaluation settings per task. Standard Setting follows real-robot conditions: the agent observes the environment only through the robot’s sensors and cannot reset it by default. The simulation waits while the agent reasons, and its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent makes decisions. Privileged Setting provides an approximate upper bound and can be used to generate training data, where the agent has access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution by trial and error. We call each <task–setting> pair a test. Tests of the same task share the initial scene and success rule, allowing us to compare success as state access, reset limits, and timing change.

Third, provide unified infrastructure for different models, harnesses, and control approaches. With a single command, EFE runs different combinations of models and harnesses across diverse robotics tasks. Given a natural-language task instruction, the agent chooses its control approach (Figure 1). In Direct control, it directly outputs actions after receiving observations [47, 191, 199]. In Code to control, it outputs a planner, controller, or other program that generates the robot’s actions [84]. In Train a policy, it trains a policy in simulation and uses it to control the robot [95, 83]. The framework enforces the access permitted by each evaluation setting, and a verifier outside the agent’s control grades every attempt [203, 196].

We evaluate eight coding agents on a core set of 456 hard tasks. The strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra [115] in Codex, solves 77% of the Privileged tests but only 30% of the Standard tests of the same 391 tasks. Apart from the three strongest agents, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, the best result comes from Kimi 3.1 Pro, which solves 9% of the Standard tests of the same 391 tasks (34 tests, Figure 10) and 7% of the Realtime tests (Figure 7). The Realtime Setting is harder still: 63% of its tests remain unsolved by any agent, compared with 50% of the Standard tests of the same 54 tasks. To identify where failures occur within a task, we divide each task into stages. Each stage corresponds to a change in the world required to complete the task. For example, the task of putting a tomato into a closed fridge has three stages: the fridge is open, the tomato is inside, and the fridge is closed again. For each failed attempt of the eight agents on 427 tasks, a separate coding agent labels the stage at which the failure occurred. Our main findings are as follows.

  • •

    Privileged versus Standard (Section 3.2). Resets help GPT-6 Astra more than the exact object state does, and with both, its success rate closes most of the gap to the Privileged Setting. Stages that need precision become much harder in the Standard Setting. At these stages, resets help, but the exact state alone does not.

  • •

    Where agents fail (Section 3.3). Failures on a task tend to happen at the same stage, usually the first stage of the task. This stage also tends to be the same in the Privileged and Standard settings. Stages that change a material or move the robot’s body have the highest failure rates.

  • •

    Differences between agents (Section 3.4). Weaker agents are much more likely than stronger agents to fail before making the required contact. In the Standard Setting, the three strongest agents solve partly different sets of tests. Switching harnesses can change a model’s success rate by up to 12 percentage points.

  • •

    How agents control the robot (Section 3.5). In the Standard and Realtime settings of a soccer task, agents trained a policy when given a GPU and a training library, and only trained policies won. Agents mostly control the robot directly in the Standard Setting and write programs to control it in the Privileged and Realtime settings.

2 The Embodied First Exam: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Coding Agents in Robotics

In this section, we describe how we evaluate coding agents on robotics tasks (Section 2.1), the resource constraints of each task (Section 2.2), and the tasks of the exam (Section 2.3).

2.1 Framework and Evaluation Protocol

Existing robotics benchmarks focus on visuomotor policy learning with a relatively fixed input-output interface, whereas we evaluate coding agents that can choose their own control approach. Our design principle is therefore to give the agent broad freedom over how it acts and to constrain only the result: we fix where it starts, what resources it gets, and how success is checked. To achieve this, we package every robotics task in the format of Harbor [44], the evaluation framework of Terminal-Bench [102], which runs the task in containers, as shown in Figure 2(a). The agent has its own workspace, where it can install packages, write and run programs, and train models. Each task starts from a fixed initial state; a verifier outside the agent’s container reports whether the agent’s answer meets the task’s success rule.

On top of this framework, we define a unified evaluation protocol with up to three settings per task (Figure 2(b)). We design Privileged as an approximate upper bound on performance, with full access to the simulator for trial and error, while Standard and Realtime make the evaluation as close to a real robot as possible. The bound holds over a set of tasks, not for every single task, because an agent can solve a task in Standard that it fails in Privileged (Appendix D). For a given task, all settings share the same initial scene, success rule, and time limit, so their results are paired. They differ in what the agent observes, whether it can reset, whether the world waits, and where the simulator and the verifier run, never in the control approach the agent may choose. We ablate the first two differences in Section 3.2.

Privileged. In Privileged, the agent runs in the same container as the simulator, so it can read the full simulation state and reset without limit. The agent must submit a low-level robot trajectory (or a controller program for some tasks). The verifier replays the trajectory (or runs the controller) in a separate container to determine task success.

Standard. In Standard, we run the simulator as a service in a separate container. Through predefined APIs, the agent has limited access to the simulator: it can query proprioceptive state (e.g., joint positions, velocities, and torques), and sensor data (e.g., calibrated RGB-D images), and send action chunks to control the robot. The simulation is paused between API requests, so the agent faces no real-time pressure. Resets are disallowed unless the task provides an explicit reset budget. The verifier grades task progress online as the agent controls the robot, and in most suites the interface reports a success to the agent and ends the episode.

Realtime. Realtime is the same as Standard, except that the simulation does not pause between agent actions but keeps running in real time; for computationally expensive tasks, it runs at a fixed fraction of real time (e.g., 0.5×\times). Due to compute constraints, we currently evaluate Realtime only on dynamic tasks. Appendix C details each setting.

2.2 Resource Constraints for Coding Agents

As shown in Figure 3, we set resource constraints for each task: a time limit and a token budget for the agent, a reset budget and, in some tasks, a step limit for the robot (RoboDojo’s own limit in Figure 3, or a cap on the episode length that the instruction states), and caps on CPU, memory, GPU memory, and disk. The token budget is high enough that no attempt reaches it. The time limit is the same in every setting of a task, and when it runs out we stop the agent and grade the result it has at that point. Resets are unlimited in Privileged. In Standard and Realtime, there are no resets unless the task grants a budget, which nine suites do, with 3 to 50 resets. We set the compute caps per task from its measured needs and monitor usage throughout the run (Appendix C).

We observe that coding agents may choose different control approaches under different resource constraints and in different settings (Figures 1 and 3.5). For example, if we provide a GPU, agents can train a policy to control the robot (Figure 18).

2.3 Task Suites

The exam contains 1,156 tasks in 35 suites. A suite is a set of related tasks on one simulator. Each task states a goal, usually in natural language, such as untying a knot or turning the page of a book with a dexterous hand, and the agent must control the robot to reach that goal. We built 9 suites with 411 tasks for the exam and adapted the other 26 suites with 745 tasks from existing robotics benchmarks. Together, the tasks use 47 robots of nine types (Table 2 in Appendix A, which lists the simulator, the robots and the number of tasks of every suite).

New suites. We built nine new suites because the adapted suites contain few tasks for several embodiments and capabilities. Most of their original benchmarks focus on visuomotor policy learning (Section 4), and 618 of their 745 tasks use single-arm, bimanual or mobile manipulators. The new suites form three groups, which are the rows of Figure 4, and Section A.1 describes each suite. RoboARC, DexHandExam and RoboPaint require contact-rich manipulation of deformable objects, multi-part assemblies and tools. RoboDynamicExam and the two Embodied Olympics suites involve moving objects and opponents, so the agent must act at the right time, and they contain most of the humanoid tasks of the exam. iSpatialGym, Embodied Safety Exam and RoboEngineer test abilities beyond executing a stated goal, since they give the goal only as an image, mix hazardous with benign requests, or require adapting a controller to hidden dynamics.

Adapted suites. The other 26 suites come from existing benchmarks, and their tasks range from language-conditioned tabletop manipulation and long-horizon household activities to humanoid whole-body control, dexterous tool use, musculoskeletal control, aerial manipulation and laboratory automation (Section A.2). For each suite, we keep the scenes, robots and success rules of the original benchmark, in some suites with a stricter success rule. We save the initial state of each task as a frozen scene, write an instruction that states every convention that the agent cannot infer and connect the suite to the interfaces of the three settings. We also remove the expert policies and demonstration data of the original benchmark, so that the agent cannot copy a known solution from its container.

Core set. We report results on a core set of 456 hard tasks (901 tests), because tasks within a suite often require similar skills and current agents already solve many of the tasks. The core set excludes tasks that we judged easy and tasks that an initial screening agent, GPT-6 Luna, solved, and it keeps every task that the authors of a suite asked to keep. Because GPT-6 Luna belongs to the same model family as GPT-6 Astra, the screening may bias the core set against tasks that this family solves. Table 2 gives the number of core tasks in each suite. Each core task also has a default setting, and the controlled runs of Section 3.2 use the default test of each core task. The default is Standard for 403 tasks and Realtime for 53 tasks in which timing is essential; one more core task also has a Realtime test. The remaining 700 tasks stay in the exam and can be run in the same way. We split 427 of the core tasks into stages, such as opening a fridge (Section 3), and Figure 5 groups the core tasks by the categories of these stages (Table 7). Relation stages, such as placing or assembling objects, are the most common, and most tasks with Dynamic, Body or Competition stages come from the new suites (86 of 99).

3 Analysis

We evaluate eight coding agents on the core set (Figure 7). Section 3.1 gives their success rates, and Sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 report four findings. An agent is a model in a harness, such as Codex [114] or Claude Code [5], at high reasoning effort, and the harness is part of what we measure (Section 3.4). Each agent makes one attempt per test, and a test is solved when the verifier passes it (Appendix B). Success rates are the results of the public leaderboard (Appendix D).

Stage-level failure labels.

The verifier decides whether an attempt passed, but not where it went wrong. We therefore split 427 of the 456 core tasks into stages in a task graph (Figure 6(a)). Its edges give the order in which the stages must be met. Each stage has a type, such as open, in one of nine categories (Table 7), and the contact it needs. Figure 6(b) shows how many stages hold during three attempts. A failed attempt has at most one failure stage: the stage of an irreversible event, such as a fall, or else of the earliest mistake that the agent did not correct. This mistake can come before the stage’s prerequisites are met, as when an agent drops the tomato before it has opened the fridge. It also has up to two failure phenomena. Claude Opus 5.5, for example, falls while carrying the milk, so it fails at stage 4 with a loss of balance. An attempt reaches a stage if it meets the stage’s condition or fails there. We analyze the failed attempts of the eight agents on these 427 tasks. GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex wrote the labels of most attempts and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in Claude Code those of the remaining attempts; Claude Sonnet 5.5 reviewed every label file (Section H.1).

3.1 Overall Results

Three agents each solve more than twice as many Standard tests as any of the other five. GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon solve 24.1% to 33.6% of the 456 Standard tests (Figure 7). We call them the three strongest agents and the other five the weaker agents. The Realtime Setting is harder than the Standard Setting. On the 54 tasks with both tests, GPT-6 Astra solves 23 Standard and 17 Realtime tests, Claude Opus 5.5 solves 10 and 4, and Gemini 4 Argon solves 15 and 5. 63% of these Realtime tests remain unsolved by any agent, compared with 50% of the Standard tests of the same tasks.

Together, the three strongest agents solve 48% of the Standard tests. Figure 8 shows the outcome of every attempt. In the Standard Setting, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon solve many tests that GPT-6 Astra fails, whereas in the Privileged Setting GPT-6 Astra alone solves nearly every test that any agent solves. The five weaker agents add only a few tests in either setting. Section 3.4 examines which tests each agent solves.

In most suites with at least five Standard tests, at least half of these tests are solved by none of the three strongest agents. This holds in 14 of these 22 suites. Of the 20 suites with at least five Privileged tests, it holds only in HumanoidBench (Figure 9). Averaged over the three strongest agents, the success rate is at least 70% in 10 Privileged suites and in no Standard suite.

3.2 What Causes the Drop from the Privileged to the Standard Setting?

Figure 10 pairs the Privileged and Standard tests of the 391 core tasks that have both. Of the 303 tasks that GPT-6 Astra solves in the Privileged Setting, it fails 191 in the Standard Setting. It solves only 4 tasks in the Standard Setting alone, and 116 (30%) in all. Its success rate drops in each of the 20 suites with at least five such tasks. Two of the features that the Standard Setting lacks are the exact state of every object and unlimited resets.

Adding resets closes more of this gap than adding the exact state. In controlled runs of GPT-6 Astra in Codex, we add one or both of two features to the Standard interface: a query for the exact state of every object, and unlimited resets with saved states (Figure 11(a), Appendix G). On the 391 core tasks that have both settings, the success rate rises from 28% to 45% with the state, to 53% with resets and to 68% with both. On their Privileged tests, it is 77%. With resets, 66% of the successes come in an episode that starts from a saved state, so the agent retries a hard stage without repeating the whole task (Section E.1).

Stages that need precision fail much more often in the Standard Setting. From the stage labels of the eight agents, we compute the failure rate of each stage type in each setting: the number of stages of the type at which attempts fail, divided by the number that attempts reach. We compare the settings within each suite (Figure 11(b)). A stage type is precise when it needs a tight fit, a target pose or path, or contact with a moving object, and coarse when it needs only a region, a container, a grasp or the state of a mechanism (Section H.5). Among the types compared in at least two suites, the failure rate rises by 24 to 46 percentage points at precise types and by 1 to 20 points at coarse types. Assembling, for example, rises from 34% to 80%, and placing from 23% to 35%. If we count only stages that the same agent reaches on the same task in both settings, the difference between the two groups remains significant: precise stages rise by 25 points and coarse stages by 15 (Section E.1). Figure 12 shows a precise stage that fails in the Standard Setting. There, Claude Opus 5.5 holds the front guard of a fan 36 to 39 degrees off the fan’s axis, where seating allows 5 degrees, and pushing it further moves the whole fan. Section H.6 gives the full attempt and two more paired examples (Figure 32).

At precise stages, resets help GPT-6 Astra, but the exact state alone does not. We take the Standard tests that GPT-6 Astra failed in the baseline run and group them by the type of the stage at which they failed (Figure 11(c)). Some of these failures would succeed in any second attempt. To estimate how many, we use a run that adds neither feature and only hides the success signal. Of the 91 failures at precise stages, this run solves 19%, the run with the state 21% and the run with resets 36%, with 31 of its 33 successes coming after a reset or a restored state. Compared with the run without the success signal, the state thus solves about two more of the 91 failures, and resets about 16 more. At coarse stages, by contrast, the state alone solves 34% of the 97 failures, against 14% for the run without the success signal (Section E.1).

3.3 At Which Stage of a Task Do Agents Fail?

Failures on a task tend to happen at the same stage. The concentration of failure stages measures this (Figure 13). For each test, it is the share of pairs of failed attempts, by different agents, that failed at the same stage. We use the attempts with a located failure stage and average this share over tests. The baseline draws each failure stage at random, with the probability of each relative position in the task taken from the failures on the other tasks of the setting (Section H.5). Over the eight agents, the concentration is 61% in the Standard Setting, against 37% for the baseline. The five weaker agents often fail before they reach any stage of a task (Section 3.4), so much of this agreement could come from failures at the first stage. We therefore check the three strongest agents separately. Over the 217 Standard tests with at least two located failures among them, the concentration is 56%, against 31% for the baseline built from their failures on the other Standard tasks. The most common failure stage of a test is usually the first stage of its task: of the 264 Standard tests whose failures have a single most common stage, it is the first stage in 65% (Section E.2). Figure 14 shows a shared stage that is not the first. In the Standard Setting, all eight agents fail this test, and seven of them catch a thrown ball in a cup and then fail, in different ways, at the recatch. In Figure 31 in Section H.6, the three strongest agents each put the first of three batteries into a bin and then tip the robot over on the way to the second, whereas four of the five weaker agents fail at the first battery.

The stage at which agents fail also tends to be the same in the two settings. We take the 188 tasks whose failures have a single most common stage in both the Privileged and the Standard Setting. In 105 of them, this stage is the first stage in both settings, and we leave these tasks out. Of the other 83 tasks, 47 (57%) have the same common stage in both settings (Figure 13). If the failure stages of each setting were drawn at random as above, this share would be 9%, again leaving out draws in which both common stages are the first stage (Section H.5).

Stages that change a material or move the robot’s body have the highest failure rates (Figure 13). The failure rate of a stage category is the number of stages at which attempts fail divided by the number that they reach, with the Privileged and Standard settings pooled. Material stages, such as wiping, fail at 66%, body stages, such as walking, at 45%, and mechanism stages, such as opening a door, at 20%. Each category occurs mostly in particular suites and with particular robots, so these rates do not show that the category itself causes the failures (Section E.2).

3.4 How Do Agents Differ?

The five weaker agents more often fail without making the required contact. In the failure profiles of Figure 15, this happens in 17% to 24% of their failed Standard and Realtime attempts, against 7% to 10% for the three strongest agents. Of their failed Standard attempts on tasks with at least two stages, they reach no stage at all in 44% to 64%, against 27% to 36% (Table 19). Counted per contact stage that they reach, the weaker agents fail without contact at 9.1% to 18.5% of these stages, against 2.7% to 3.7% (Table 19). Figure 16 shows a BEHAVIOR-1K test, preparing a lunch box, that all eight agents failed in the Standard Setting. The three strongest agents each packed three or four foods, Kimi 3.1 Pro packed two, and the other four weaker agents none. Section H.6 describes the attempts and two more tests (Figure 30). GPT-6.1 Sol, which wrote most of the labels, is from the same family as GPT-6 Astra, which could bias these comparisons (Section H.5).

The three strongest agents succeed on partly different tests. In the Standard Setting, no agent’s solved tests are a subset of another agent’s (Figure 15). GPT-6 Astra solves 59% of Claude Opus 5.5’s solved Standard tests and 66% of Gemini 4 Argon’s. In the Privileged Setting, these shares are 92% and 95% (Figure 22). Between them, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon solve 64 Standard tests that GPT-6 Astra fails. Each agent made one attempt per test, so part of this difference may come from the variation between runs. Of the 69 Standard tests that at least one weaker agent solves, the three strongest agents solve 65. For each weaker agent, 93% to 100% of its solved tests are also solved by at least one agent above it in Figure 7, as the last column of Figure 15 shows (Section E.3).

The harness also changes the result (Figure 15). We ran GPT-6 Astra in Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5 in Codex, and Gemini 4 Argon in both. On the 456 core tests of the Standard Setting, GPT-6 Astra solves 34% in Codex and 22% in Claude Code. Gemini 4 Argon solves 29% in Codex, 25% in Claude Code and 24% in its own Antigravity CLI, and Claude Opus 5.5 solves 26% in Codex and 25% in Claude Code. Cross-provider runs go through an adapter (Appendix G). Antigravity CLI ends the session when Gemini’s content filter blocks a reply, which may explain part of Gemini 4 Argon’s gap (Section E.3).

3.5 Which Control Approach Do Agents Use?

In the Standard and Realtime settings of a soccer task, agents trained a policy when given a GPU and a training library, and only trained policies won. The soccer match of Embodied Olympics - Match comes in two versions with the same frozen scene and opponent (Figure 17(b)). In both, the agent controls two humanoid robots joint by joint, so it needs a walking gait. The GPU version adds a GPU, a reinforcement-learning library, GPU copies of the match for training and an example of training in its instruction. On this version, 10 of 12 attempts trained a policy with reinforcement learning in the Standard Setting, and 7 of 8 did in the Realtime Setting. Three attempts won in the Standard Setting and one in the Realtime Setting, all with a trained policy. On the CPU version, agents wrote gaits by hand, and none of the 12 Standard and 8 Realtime attempts won. The Standard counts include the runs of the harness comparison, so some models appear more than once (Table 4). In the Privileged Setting, agents also won on the CPU version, but every win there reused the opponent’s walking network. The two versions differ in several ways, and this one task cannot show which difference matters. GPT-6 Astra, for example, trained policies and won 10–8 with the GPU, and tuned a hand-written gait and lost 3–13 without it (Figure 18).

In the Standard Setting, agents mostly control the robot directly, and in the Privileged and Realtime settings they mostly write programs (Figure 17(a)). A coding agent labeled the control approach of 1,489 sampled attempts (Section E.4). Where the simulation pauses between requests, 61% of the sampled Standard attempts send one action chunk at a time and look at the camera images or sensor readings before choosing the next. With the full state, 82% of the Privileged attempts compute the motion in a program. When the clock keeps running, 97% of the Realtime attempts use a program, and in 82% the program runs the control loop. Six of the 1,489 attempts were labeled as training a policy.

4 Related Work

This section reviews the closest lines of work. Appendix K gives an extended review.

Benchmarks for coding agents.

Coding agents and other language-model agents are evaluated mostly on digital tasks, such as resolving issues in real repositories [64, 104], completing tasks in a terminal [102], machine learning engineering and research [14, 143], and operating websites and desktop applications [198, 168]. The interface between the model and the computer affects how often an agent succeeds [174], and other work measures how often agents exploit the tests that grade them [196]. The Embodied First Exam extends these evaluations to robotics tasks. In its Standard and Realtime settings, the agent must interpret sensor observations and often cannot undo an action. In every setting, a program that the agent cannot change grades each attempt.

Language models for robots.

Language models have been used to sequence skills into plans [1, 54], to write robot programs that call perception and control primitives [84], to specify value maps or keypoint constraints that a planner turns into motions [53, 52], and to write reward functions [95]. Most of these systems pair a model with an interface designed for it. The Embodied First Exam evaluates unchanged general-purpose coding agents on the whole loop of reading an interface, choosing a control approach, carrying it out and revising it. In embodied benchmarks for language models [139, 78, 176], the model chooses from an action space that the benchmark defines. The exam gives the agent the robot’s control interface, so the agent also decides how its actions are produced.

Agentic robots and their harnesses.

Recent work runs general-purpose agents on robots [125] with the three control approaches of Figure 1. In direct control, GPT-6 Astra serves as the policy on manipulation benchmarks [191, 199, 61]. In code to control, coding agents write programs for simulated and real robots [150, 62, 50, 56], often with skill libraries or other added tools [93, 48]. In train a policy, agents train policies in the real world or in simulation [165, 83]. Most of these studies fix the control approach in advance. The exam supports all three approaches and leaves the choice to the agent. Harnesses for these agents differ in the action interface they provide [18, 34, 23], in whether the agent can call learned policies as tools [80, 33], and in the support they add for tracking state and checking outcomes [157, 30]. The exam runs each harness unmodified with the models of its own provider, and through an adapter with other providers’ models (Appendix G), so different harnesses can be compared on the same tasks.

Benchmarks for robots.

Most robotics benchmarks focus on visuomotor policy learning and evaluate learned policies, such as vision-language-action models [11, 69, 10, 38], on manipulation, household and humanoid tasks [87, 17, 76, 106, 132]. A learned policy receives only a fixed set of observations. A coding agent can run any program on its computer, so the exam adds rules about what the agent may access (Section 2.1) and adapts 26 existing benchmarks (Section A.2). Benchmarks for agentic robots have also appeared. CaP-X [32] varies the level of abstraction of the primitives that coding agents compose, RobotWorld [178] spans manipulation, locomotion, driving and aerial control, and EmbodiedSWE [134] and BiGym 2.0 [194] evaluate coding agents on dexterous and humanoid tasks. The Embodied First Exam covers 47 robots of nine types. It also separates what an agent can do with full access to the simulator from what it can do through the robot’s sensors alone.

5 Conclusion

We introduced the Embodied First Exam, a unified evaluation framework that connects any coding agent to simulated robots and lets the agent execute actions in three ways. The exam contains 1,156 tasks on 47 robots. On the 391 hard core tasks that have both settings, the strongest agent reaches a success rate of 77% in the Privileged Setting but only 30% in the Standard Setting. In controlled runs with this agent, adding unlimited resets closes more of this gap than adding the exact object state, and at stages that need precision, resets help but the exact state alone does not. Failures on a task tend to happen at the same stage, weaker agents are much more likely than stronger agents to fail before making the required contact, and in the Standard and Realtime settings of a soccer task, agents trained a policy when given a GPU and a training library, and only trained policies won. The strongest agent already solves most tasks when it has full access to the simulator, but in the Standard and Realtime settings, which are designed to mirror how a real robot is deployed and tested, it still has much room for improvement.

Future work.

Running each core test several times will separate failures that an agent repeats from failures of a single run, and it will give confidence intervals for the comparisons between agents and between settings. We will also add more Realtime tasks, since the Realtime Setting has the largest share of tests that no agent solves. Finally, because the Standard Setting gives the agent only the robot’s sensor readings and control interface, the same interface can be used on physical hardware once there is a way to grade the outcome. In a first demonstration, two agents played a buzz wire game with a physical robot arm (Appendix I), and we plan to evaluate agents on real robots systematically through this interface.

Limitations.

Each agent makes a single attempt per test, the stage-level and control-approach labels come from agents, and all results are in simulation. Appendix J discusses these and further limitations.

Appendix A Suites and Tasks

What a task contains.

We package every task in the Harbor format with a fixed directory structure. The file instruction.md gives the agent its prompt: the goal, the submission requirements, the limits, and every convention the agent cannot infer, including coordinate frames, units, the action layout, how to use the robot client, and the reset budget. Any goal specified as an image, video, or other file is placed inside the agent’s container and named in instruction.md. We store the task configuration in task.toml, which specifies the time limit, the CPU, memory, and disk caps of the agent’s container, the verifier settings, and task metadata (the simulator, the robot, and whether a reference solution exists). The environment/ directory defines the runtime via a Dockerfile for the agent’s workspace container and a docker-compose.yaml that adds the remaining containers (the simulator service in Standard and Realtime, and a resource monitor) along with their resource caps. Within it, environment/instance.json defines the frozen scene (the objects, the robot, and their initial state), which the simulator checks against a stored hash at every build and reset so every episode starts from the same state. The tests/ directory contains the verifier: its own Dockerfile and docker-compose.yaml, the entry script test.sh, and the grading code with the success rule, all running in an isolated container that the agent never sees. When a task has a reference solution, we include solution/solve.sh, which validates the task and is never shown to the agent, and we provide README.md to describe the task for human readers. Finally, we pin every base image to a fixed tag or digest so every run of a task uses the exact same software.

Table 1 gives the size of the exam, and Table 2 lists its 35 suites, of which 9 were built for the exam and 26 are adapted from existing benchmarks, whose scenes, robots and success rules we keep. The Robots column counts distinct robot models in the suite. The same robot can appear in several suites, so the total counts each of the 47 robots once. A test is one task in one setting, and the Core column counts the tasks in the core set. Time limits range from 30 minutes to four hours by suite. Of the 1,156 tasks, 590 allow one hour and 351 allow two hours or more.

A.1 New Suites

RoboARC, DexHandExam and RoboPaint require contact-rich manipulation of deformable objects, multi-part assemblies and tools. In RoboARC, single- and dual-arm robots untie knots, thread ropes through holes, disentangle rings from wire puzzles, guide a loop along a wire without touching it, and assemble IKEA furniture. Earlier work studied such tasks with dedicated systems for untangling cables [152] and with datasets of furniture assembly manuals [158]. In DexHandExam, dexterous hands turn book pages, open jars and insert a USB stick, and objects move only through contact and gravity. In RoboPaint, a robot arm reproduces a painting or a calligraphy character with a brush or a pen, so the task tests fine tool control. Dedicated robot painters such as FRIDA [129] plan their strokes in a differentiable simulation of the painting process.

RoboDynamicExam and the two Embodied Olympics suites involve dynamic objects and opponents, so the agent has to act under tight timing constraints. These three suites contain 53 of the 86 tasks that have a Realtime test. RoboDynamicExam asks single- and dual-arm robots to catch, strike and hand over moving objects such as tossed balls and sliding pucks. In Embodied Olympics - Fun, a humanoid performs athletic skills in 79 task families, such as dribbling a ball through a slalom, and in Embodied Olympics - Match, robots play full matches of table tennis, badminton, soccer, foosball or fencing against scripted or learned opponents. Robots have learned to play table tennis [26], badminton [97] and soccer [43] with reinforcement learning and task-specific training.

The remaining three suites test abilities beyond executing a stated goal. In iSpatialGym, a mobile bimanual robot receives the goal only as an image of what its head camera should show when the task is done, and it must rearrange the scene or reposition itself until its camera view matches this goal image. Multimodal models have been evaluated on spatial reasoning by answering questions about videos of indoor scenes [173], and iSpatialGym requires the agent to act on such reasoning. Embodied Safety Exam pairs hazardous requests, whose literal execution would cause harm, with benign requests of the same kind, so the agent must refuse the hazardous requests and complete the benign ones, even when the hazard is hidden or emerges during the task. Its verifier decides success from what physically happens in the simulation. RoboEngineer asks the agent to tune a controller on a nominal simulator that it can access, deploy the controller to an evaluation simulator with undisclosed dynamics and refine it from the deployment feedback. This loop resembles sim-to-real transfer, which prior work addresses with domain and dynamics randomization [148, 118] and by aligning simulated with real physics [46]. RoboEngineer’s drone tasks build on the learned dynamics models of Neural Lander and Neural-Fly [135, 117], and its racing-car tasks port the MuJoCo vehicle model of AnyCar [166], a wheeled car, without its learned dynamics model.

A.2 Adapted Suites

The other 26 suites come from existing benchmarks, and we group them by their main embodiment, as Figure 4 (right) also does. The single-arm suites are LIBERO-MAX [193], RoboLab [172], MetaWorld+ [99], VLABench [190], ManiGuard [119], EmbodiedSWE [134], LabUtopia [79], MolmoSpaces [71] and AutoBio [74], and they range from language-conditioned tabletop manipulation to laboratory automation. The bimanual suites are RoboDojo [16], RoboTwin 2.0 [17], ABC Sim [4], RoboWits [85] and YAMLab [8], and the mobile manipulation suites are BEHAVIOR-1K [76], RoboCasa365 [107], RoboCasa [106] and KinDER [55]. The first three include long-horizon household activities in house and kitchen scenes, and KinDER tests physical reasoning. RoboCasa-GR1 [110], BiGym 2.0 [194] and HumanoidBench [132] cover humanoid manipulation and whole-body control. DexToolBench [65] and DexJoCo [155] cover dexterous manipulation and tool use. MyoSuite [13] covers musculoskeletal control, MuJoCo Playground [187] covers quadruped locomotion together with a few arm tasks, and AM-Bench [162] covers aerial manipulation.

Appendix B Protocol Details

Budgets.

Each attempt runs in a container with 2 to 16 CPU cores and 4 to 39 GiB of memory, with a GPU where the simulator or the task needs one, with a wall-clock limit of 30 minutes to four hours, depending on the suite, and with a token budget that no attempt reaches. The harness can reach only the API of its model and the package registries, except in Embodied Olympics - Fun, which runs with open network access. The harness’s web search is off in every task. A proxy between the harness and the model provider forwards only the requests to the model’s API.

Reference solutions and integrity checks.

Every task must fail when the robot does nothing and pass with its reference solution wherever one exists (686 tasks have a full reference solution, and 78 have a partial one). Tasks without a reference solution rely on the original success rule and a human review. Reference solutions never enter the agent’s container, and the solutions of the original benchmarks are removed from the container images. Before a suite is added, an agent is instructed to pass its tasks without solving them. If the agent succeeds on any task, the suite is not added until its verifier is fixed.

Leaderboard rules.

Each agent makes one attempt per test. An attempt that ends with an infrastructure or API error is rerun, and the latest finished attempt counts. A test counts as solved when the verifier reports success for its attempt. We report each setting over all of its core tests, including those of Embodied Olympics - Fun, whose tasks run with open network access, and of the suites with their own runtime, Embodied Olympics - Match and RoboEngineer, and Figure 9 gives the results by suite. The harness comparison uses the 456 core tests of the Standard Setting. When we pool the three strongest agents, as in Sections 3.1 and D, each test counts once per agent, and rates are reported per attempt.

Approach labels.

For Section 3.5, an agent read the logs of a random sample of 1,489 attempts and assigned each attempt the approach that produced its graded answer. Code to control covers three kinds of program. An open-loop program computes the whole motion in advance, as waypoints, key frames, inverse-kinematics solutions or a recorded sequence, and runs it without feedback. A closed-loop program reads the state or the cameras at every control step or action chunk and adjusts its commands. A parameter search finds a passing motion, or its parameters, by trying many episodes and resets or by running an optimizer such as the cross-entropy method (CEM), CMA-ES, or a grid or random search. In Direct control, the agent sends one action chunk at a time and decides on the next one after looking at images or readings. In Train a policy, the agent first trains a control policy, such as a neural network or a reinforcement-learning policy, which then controls the robot. Attempts that switched approach midway or used two approaches equally are labeled mixed, and attempts that only explored or never ran anything are labeled as having no control plan. Figure 1 shows an example of each approach.

Appendix C Interface, Grading and Physics

This section expands Section 2.1 with the protocol rules and each suite’s values and examples.

C.1 Interface

Privileged Setting: a simulator library in the agent’s container.

The agent’s container holds the simulator of the suite and a small Python library that the exam provides, which we call the tooling. The tooling rebuilds the frozen scene, resets it, advances it by applying actions, reads the state of every object and records each applied action as one row of an array. The agent may also call the planning primitives of the original benchmark, such as the grasp and place primitives of RoboTwin 2.0 with its CuRobo planner, or write its own planner, optimizer or learned controller. Whatever the agent calls, the tooling records the low-level action row applied at every control step, and the answer is this array of actions, saved as a trajectory file. For RoboTwin 2.0, for example, a row has 34 columns (16 joint position targets, 16 joint velocity targets and two gripper commands) and one row is applied per 4 ms physics step. In the Privileged tests of Embodied Olympics - Match and EmbodiedSWE the answer is instead a program (one that plays the match, or one that controls the robot through the task), and the verifier runs it in a fresh simulator.

Standard Setting: the simulator as a service.

In the Standard and Realtime settings, the simulator runs as the simulator service in a separate container that the agent cannot access. The agent reaches it over HTTP through a Python client library that the exam provides. One call returns the specification of the robot: the action types with their layouts, units and limits; every joint with its position, velocity and effort limits and drive gains; the grippers and tool frames; the cameras with their intrinsics and mounting; the layout of the joint readings; the conventions of the world frame; and the budgets. A second call returns observations: either the current camera images, without advancing the simulation, or the images after the simulation has run for a requested number of seconds with the last command held. A third call executes an action chunk of TT rows, each of dimension dd, and returns the video of the execution. Where the service offers it, a fourth computes forward and inverse kinematics on the model of the robot without advancing physics. A reset call exists only in tasks that grant resets. Every response contains the camera images (RGB, and depth on request), one row of joint readings per image (joint positions and velocities, gripper opening, tool pose and an estimate of the drive effort), the camera calibration, the simulated time and the time the agent has left. Object poses, segmentation, scene files, the seed and the success rule are never sent. Contact forces on objects are not sent either, except as safety telemetry that a suite documents field by field, as in RoboARC, and that never gives an object’s pose. Any other request, such as a query for object states or for success, returns an error. The images come back as binary data that the agent’s code can store and process, so they do not have to pass through the model’s context.

From a chunk to motion.

Joint position rows are d​tdt seconds apart, where d​tdt is a multiple of the control period and at most 0.5 s. The service rejects a value of d​tdt that breaks this rule and does not round it. The service streams the rows to the drives of the joints in the way a position controller on a real robot follows a trajectory, either interpolating between rows or holding each row until the next. It clips any value outside the joint limits and reports each clipped entry in the response. End-effector rows go through the inverse kinematics or the motion planner of the suite. Where the original benchmark controls the robot through a higher-level controller, the agent sends the commands of that controller, as in RoboCasa and in the whole-body controller of BiGym 2.0. Each suite keeps its own control rate and physics step. Control rates range from 5 Hz (the mobile robot in MolmoSpaces) to 500 Hz (AutoBio, where one row is one 2 ms physics step), and one control step runs up to 100 physics steps (VLABench). The success rule is checked after every action chunk and every observation request that advances physics, and in most suites the first success ends the episode. In the Standard tests of RoboDojo, a success does not end the episode, so that the end of the episode does not tell the agent that it has succeeded, which would give it a success check to try against until it passes. The episode ends at the task’s step limit, when the agent ends it, at its time limit, or when a check of the task fails, and it passes if the success rule held at any point, which matches RoboDojo’s own success within its step limit.

Realtime Setting: a simulation that keeps running.

The Realtime Setting uses the same calls. From the first request that advances physics, the simulation advances one control step every SS control periods of wall-clock time, whatever the agent does, where S≥1S\geq 1 is a slowdown factor that each task states. A submitted chunk is answered at once and replaces the queued actions starting at a control step that the agent specifies. When the queue is empty, the robot holds its last target. The agent can therefore run a program in its own container that observes the robot and sends new chunks in a loop. By default, SS is 1 when the simulator runs at least three times faster than real time, and larger otherwise, so that the service can run each step on time. The service records the steps it could not run on time, and the time the robot stood still because of them.

Suites with their own runtime.

RoboEngineer and Embodied Olympics - Match use their own runtime instead of the simulator service, in their Standard tests and in the Realtime tests of Embodied Olympics - Match. In RoboEngineer, the agent tunes a controller in a simulator that the agent can access and deploys the controller to a second simulator, which the agent cannot access and whose dynamics differ from those of the first in ways not disclosed to the agent. The verifier then scores the controller that the agent selects on episodes that the agent has not seen.

Step limits and time budgets.

The protocol adds no step limit to the Standard and Realtime settings. RoboDojo keeps its own step limit (Figure 3), and many other suites cap the episode length, which the instruction states. A Privileged trajectory may have at most a stated number of rows. The main limit is the agent’s wall-clock time, from 30 minutes to four hours depending on the suite, and it is the same in every setting of a task. Each response reports the time left, counted from the first request of the agent. One call may return only a stated number of images and may run for at most 15 minutes by default, so that one call cannot exhaust the memory of the service or occupy it indefinitely.

Limits.

The limits of a test are the agent’s wall-clock time and token budget, the resets that the task grants, the slowdown SS in the Realtime Setting, the per-call limits above, and the CPU, memory, process, disk and GPU memory caps of each container, which a resource monitor records and enforces where the container runtime does not. Privileged tests allow unlimited resets, and Standard and Realtime tests allow no resets unless the task grants a budget, which its instruction states (Section 2.2). These values are part of the configuration of a result, and results are compared only between runs with the same configuration.

C.2 Grading

Success rules.

Each task is graded by one success rule, a condition on the simulator state. Adapted suites keep the success rule of the original benchmark and tighten it in some tasks. Examples are the success function of a RoboTwin 2.0 task, the BDDL goal of a BEHAVIOR-1K activity evaluated on OmniGibson object states, and the solved flag of MyoSuite. For the suites that we built, we wrote our own rules on the simulator state. The success rule of Embodied Olympics - Fun checks the suite’s scoring checkpoints, legal contacts and fouls after every 1 ms physics step, RoboDynamicExam checks ordered phases (a catch, a hold, a crossing, a release) after every 1 ms physics step, and DexHandExam computes its checkpoints from contact pairs and contact forces. The instruction states each condition of the success rule with the same thresholds that the rule uses.

Settle and hold windows.

Some rules are checked over a time window. A hold window requires the goal to hold for a stated time, so that an object in flight or a grasp that is about to slip does not count. In BEHAVIOR-1K the goal must hold for 1 s with the object released and at rest. MyoSuite requires its solved flag for 1 s (5 s for the Baoding balls), BiGym 2.0 requires its goal for 1 s and no fall during the episode, and ManiGuard requires its goal for 10 consecutive control steps and no safety violation during the episode. A settle window keeps the simulation running with the last command held while the rule is checked, as in RoboLab, which holds the last command for 2 s. Rules without a window are checked on a single state. A window is part of the rule of the task and applies in every setting. It is checked on the live simulator in the Standard and Realtime settings and after the last row of the replay in the Privileged Setting.

Privileged Setting: a fresh replay.

The verifier rebuilds the frozen scene in a fresh process, checks that its initial state matches the stored hash, replays the submitted actions open loop and applies the success rule to the replay. By default it replays once. In BEHAVIOR-1K, AM-Bench, RoboDojo and RoboLab, whose simulators do not replay bit for bit, it replays up to three times, each in a fresh process, and the attempt passes if any replay succeeds. Where the answer is a program, as in Embodied Olympics - Match and EmbodiedSWE, the verifier runs the program in a fresh simulator instead. Because only the actions are replayed, a change that the agent made directly to the state of its own simulator, such as moving an object directly, has no effect on the result. A file that is not a valid trajectory fails.

Standard and Realtime settings: the live episode.

The simulator service checks the success rule on the episode that it ran, and the verifier reports the result from the service’s record of the episode. The service checks the hash of the start state when the episode begins and after every reset. When the agent’s time is up, the program that runs the evaluation stops every process in the agent’s container before it signals the service. From then on the service refuses every request that would advance the simulator, runs any settle window, checks the success rule on the live simulator and writes the result with the recorded trajectory. The verifier reports that result, and nothing is replayed to decide it. The result depends only on the state of the simulator, never on what the agent reports. An episode in which the agent’s actions cause a simulator error fails. A failure of the infrastructure, such as a scene that does not rebuild to its stored start state or a service that crashed, gives no result, and the whole attempt can be rerun. With resets, only the last episode is graded. We also record whether the first episode, before any reset, succeeded, and report this as first-episode success.

Isolation.

The verifier runs in its own container, built from the task’s grading files, without network, and receives only the files that the task declares for grading: the trajectory file (or the submitted program) in the Privileged Setting and the record of the simulator service, which checks the success rule, in the Standard and Realtime settings. It first removes from the agent’s output directory every entry that is not a regular file, such as a link. No writable volume is shared between the agent’s container and the containers of the simulator service and the verifier, and the simulator service opens no port on the host. The agent can never read the reference solution or the files of the verifier, and in the Standard and Realtime settings it cannot read the code of the success rule either. A program submitted as the answer runs under a user account without administrator rights and without network, cannot read the files of the simulator or the verifier, and every process it starts ends before the result is written. The result is written before the video of the attempt is rendered, and the video never changes it.

C.3 Physics

Simulators.

Each suite keeps the simulator of its original benchmark, and new suites use the simulator that suits their physics. MuJoCo [149] runs most suites, directly or through robosuite, dm_control and MyoSuite, in versions 3.2 to 3.14 and mostly on the CPU. NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab with PhysX run RoboLab, RoboDojo, YAMLab, AM-Bench, LabUtopia and EmbodiedSWE, and OmniGibson on Isaac Sim runs BEHAVIOR-1K, ManiGuard and iSpatialGym. SAPIEN 3 with PhysX runs RoboTwin 2.0, and through ManiSkill 3 it also runs RoboPaint and RoboDynamicExam. Genesis runs RoboWits. RoboEngineer runs MuJoCo, and its drone tasks add learned dynamics models, a learned ground-effect model of a quadrotor and a wind-force model fitted to published flight logs.

What is simulated.

All suites simulate rigid bodies with frictional contact, joint limits and actuator limits. Several also simulate deformable and particle matter: cloth in the blanket tasks of RoboARC (a deterministic GPU solver) and the folding tasks of RoboDojo (GPU PhysX), ropes and cords as soft bodies in RoboARC, liquids as GPU PhysX particles in RoboDojo, and the object states of OmniGibson in BEHAVIOR-1K, where objects can be sliced, cooked or filled with particles. MyoSuite moves its limbs with simulated muscles instead of motors, and RoboPaint models brushes and pens on paper. Physics steps range from 1 ms (Embodied Olympics - Fun and RoboDynamicExam) to 1/60 s (LabUtopia), with 2 ms in DexHandExam, DexJoCo and AutoBio and 1/120 s in iSpatialGym, ManiGuard, AM-Bench and YAMLab.

Determinism.

Privileged grading replays the submitted actions, so when we build a task we check whether fresh replays of a trajectory end in the same final state on the hardware used for evaluation. Where they do not, the verifier replays up to three times (Section C.2). The frozen scene is also rebuilt and checked against its stored start-state hash before every episode. Where a task does not replay reliably at all, as with the GPU cloth and liquids of RoboDojo, the task is offered only in the Standard Setting, where the live episode is graded, and its video is a recording of the live episode rather than a replay.

Realism rules.

The robot moves only through its own actuators and the controllers stated in the task. In the Standard and Realtime settings the agent has no way to set the state of the simulator, and in the Privileged Setting only actions are replayed, so moving an object directly has no effect on the grade in any setting. The suites we built for the exam add stricter rules. In Embodied Olympics - Fun, the simulator never attaches a held object rigidly to the hand, never pins a body or moves it with a motion-capture constraint, and never sets a velocity directly after the start. Balls come from ball machines and goalkeepers are force-limited mechanisms. Each robot uses its own hands and actuators, modeled on measured actuator data from the manufacturer (torque-speed curves, rotor inertia and friction). Where we increased a parameter above the manufacturer’s value, the increase is at most a factor of 1.5 to 2 and is stated in the task; the one stated exception is the grip on the high bar. DexHandExam has no rigid attachments or scripted object motion, so objects move only through contact and gravity, and in the furniture assembly tasks of RoboARC, the robot holds parts only by finger friction. Where a suite keeps a grasp aid, its documentation states it. In the knot, ring and rope tasks of RoboARC, a rigid attachment holds a grasped object and slips when the pull exceeds 60 to 65 N for 20 ms. Adapted suites keep the grasp model of the original benchmark, such as the assisted grasping of OmniGibson and the hand of MetaWorld+, which a motion-capture constraint moves.

Appendix D Additional Results

This section describes the agents, the counting rules and the data behind Section 3. It then shows the success rates of Figure 7 as bars and gives further results by suite, by cost and by task type (Section 3.1).

Agents.

We evaluate eight agents, each a model running in a harness at high reasoning effort. The three strongest are GPT-6 Astra [115] in Codex [114], Claude Opus 5.5 [7] in Claude Code [5] and Gemini 4 Argon in Antigravity CLI. The other five are Kimi 3.1 Pro and Qwen3.8 Max in Claude Code and three Flash-class models: Gemini 3.8 Flash in Antigravity CLI, GLM 5.3 Flash in Claude Code and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in DeepSeek Harness (dsh), DeepSeek’s own harness. We report each result for a model in a particular harness, because the way the harness exposes tools, manages the context and ends a session is part of what we measure. Switching harnesses can change a model’s success rate by up to 12 percentage points (Section 3.4).

Counting rules.

Appendix B gives the leaderboard rules. Each column of Figure 7 covers all core tests of one setting (456 Standard, 391 Privileged and 54 Realtime tests), and every core task has a Standard test. When we pool the three strongest agents, each test counts once per agent. For results by suite, we treat the IKEA assembly tasks of RoboARC as a separate suite.

Data.

Success rates are the results of the public leaderboard. The controlled runs add features of the Privileged Setting to the Standard Setting or run a model in a different harness.

Success rate of each agent.

Figure 19 shows the success rates of Figure 7 as bars, for each setting. GPT-6 Astra leads in every column and solves a third of the Standard tests. The three strongest agents keep the same order in every column except the Realtime column, where Gemini 4 Argon is ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. Outside the core set, success rates are higher.

Paired outcomes.

Figure 10 in Section 3.2 splits the 391 core tasks that have both a Privileged and a Standard test by the settings in which each agent solves them. GPT-6 Astra solves 4 tasks in the Standard Setting but not in the Privileged Setting, and Gemini 4 Argon solves 18 such tasks. The Privileged result is therefore an approximate upper bound on the Standard result over a set of tasks, not on each single task (Section 2.1).

Results by suite.

GPT-6 Astra leads or ties in most suites, while Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon each lead in some (Figure 9). We count only suites with at least five tests in the setting. In the Standard Setting, at least half of the tests are solved by none of the three strongest agents in 14 of 22 suites, among them DexToolBench, the IKEA assembly tasks, HumanoidBench and BEHAVIOR-1K. The three strongest agents solve at least 60% of their attempts only in ManiGuard, whose safety rules are stated in the instruction. In the Privileged Setting, at least half of the tests are unsolved only in HumanoidBench, and the three strongest agents solve at least 70% of their attempts in 10 of 20 suites: Embodied Olympics - Match, EmbodiedSWE, RoboDynamicExam, RoboCasa365, RoboWits, MuJoCo Playground, Embodied Olympics - Fun, BiGym 2.0, RoboPaint and ManiGuard.

Cost of an attempt.

Figure 20 prices each attempt from the tokens that its harness logged, at the providers’ list prices of November 2026. These are list-price costs, not billed costs. Each graded attempt is priced from the run that the leaderboard counts for it. In the Standard Setting, an attempt of GPT-6 Astra costs $27.1 on average, about four times as much as one of Claude Opus 5.5 or Gemini 4 Argon. Kimi 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3.8 Flash spend more per attempt than these two agents and solve less than half as many Standard tests. For every agent, in the Privileged and in the Standard Setting, the median failed attempt costs more than the median solved attempt.

Results by task type.

A task type describes a core task as a whole, whereas the stage-level failure labels of Section 3 assign a type to each stage of a task. By task type (Figure 21), GPT-6 Astra’s lead on the Standard tests is widest in the Tool Use and Precision & Contact types, and Gemini 4 Argon is ahead of it in Object Transport, at 39%. For the three strongest agents together, Object Transport has the highest success rate of the nine task types, at 38% of their attempts, and Tool Use has the lowest, at 11%.

Appendix E Further Analysis

This section gives the full analyses behind the key takeaways of Sections 3.2, 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5, in the same order. The definitions and statistics that these analyses use are in Appendices G and H.

E.1 Causes of the Drop from the Privileged to the Standard Setting

To measure how much two features that the Standard Setting lacks contribute to the drop, we ran GPT-6 Astra in Codex on the default tests of the core tasks with one or both of them added to the Standard interface (Figure 11(a), Appendix G). The first feature is a query that returns the state of every object, including its pose, size and velocity. The second is unlimited resets together with calls that save the simulator state and restore it later. On the 391 core tasks that have both settings, GPT-6 Astra solves 28% with the unmodified interface. The state query raises this rate to 45%, and unlimited resets raise it to 53%. With both features, the agent solves 68%, against 77% on their Privileged tests. With unlimited resets, GPT-6 Astra uses saved states to retry a hard stage without repeating the whole task. Of the 206 successes of the reset run on these tasks, 14% came in the first episode, and 66% came in an episode that started from a saved state.

The stage labels show at which kinds of stages the Standard Setting raises the failure rate (Figure 11(b)). The failure rate of a stage type is the number of its stages at which attempts fail, divided by the number of its stages that attempts reach. We compare it between the two settings within each suite and average over the suites (Table 12). Section H.5 defines the precise and coarse groups of stage types and gives the statistical tests. Among the stage types compared in at least two suites, the failure rate rises by 24 to 46 percentage points for precise types and by 1 to 20 points for coarse types. The failure rate of cleaning, which is in neither group, also rises by 51 points. Pooled within suites, the failure rate rises from 22% to 56% at precise stages and from 22% to 38% at coarse stages. Figure 12 shows an example, and Section H.6 gives it in full. The difference between the two groups is smaller, but still significant, when the same agent reaches the same stage of a task in both settings. There, the rise is 25 points at precise stages and 15 points at coarse stages. At follow-path stages, most of them waypoints of DexToolBench, the rate rises by 11 points in this comparison. Without these stages, the rise at precise stages is 33 points.

Combining the controlled runs with the stage labels shows which feature helps at which kind of stage (Figure 11(c), Table 14). We take the Standard tests that GPT-6 Astra failed in the baseline run of the controlled runs and group them by the type of the failure stage. Of these failures, 91 are at precise stages and 97 are at coarse stages. Some of these failures would turn into successes if the test were simply run again. We therefore compare each run with the run without the success signal, a further controlled run in which the interface no longer reports when an episode succeeds. This run repeats the same tests and changes only the success signal, so we use it as a rough approximation of a second attempt. Its success rate is within 4 points of the baseline’s (Table 5), but this run does not separate the variation between attempts from the effect of hiding the success signal. At precise stages, the state query solves 21% of the failures, against 19% for the run without the success signal. Unlimited resets solve 36%, and 31 of these 33 successes came after a reset or a restored state. The agent did call the state query in the runs that offer it. At precise stages, adding the state query to the resets raises the share solved from 36% to 47%. At coarse stages, the state query alone solves 34% of the failures, against 14% for the run without the success signal, and the two features together solve 67%, against 60% in the Privileged Setting. With both features, the agent solves 47% of the precise failures, compared with 73% in the Privileged Setting, and most of this remaining gap lies at follow-path, thread and assemble stages. Neither added feature lets the agent advance the physics one step at a time or call planning primitives, as the Privileged Setting does, and these abilities may account for part of the remaining gap.

The comparisons in this subsection have limits. The controlled runs use one agent. The labels cannot separate errors of perception from errors of control (Section H.5).

E.2 Where Agents Fail

Failures on a task tend to happen at the same stage (Figure 13). We measure this by the concentration of failure stages, which is the probability that two of the failed attempts on a test, chosen at random, failed at the same stage. Each agent makes one attempt per test, so the two attempts always come from different agents, and the measure pools the agents that failed the test. On the Standard tests that at least two agents failed at located stages, on tasks with at least two stages, the concentration averages 61%, and we compare it with two baselines. In the first baseline, each agent fails at a stage chosen at random, with the probability of each stage position set by how often failures occur at that position on the other tasks of the same setting, so early stages are more likely. This baseline gives 37%. In the second baseline, an agent fails at each stage with the failure rate of the stage’s type on the other tasks, and this baseline gives 48% (Table 16). For the three strongest agents alone, the concentration is 56%, against 31% for the first baseline built from their failures on the other tasks (Section H.5). Failures therefore concentrate more than the stage types predict. The most common failure stage is usually the first stage of the task. Of the 264 Standard tests whose failures have a single most common stage, this stage is the first stage in 65%, and it is the first stage in 56% of those whose tasks have at least two types of stages. In a RoboDynamicExam task, for example, seven of the eight Standard attempts caught a thrown ball in a cup and then failed at the recatch, in three different ways (Figure 14, with all eight attempts in Section H.6).

Failure rates differ between stage categories (Figure 13). Pooled over the Privileged and Standard settings, attempts fail at 66% of the material stages (such as wiping or pouring) that they reach, at 45% of the body stages (such as walking or keeping balance) and at 20% of the mechanism stages. Within a category, the rate also depends on how the robot must act. Opening a door or a lid fails in 38% of cases, whereas closing one fails in 19% when it does not already hold at the start (Section H.5), and pressing fails in 3% (Table 18). Relation stages, which place or fit one object relative to another (Table 7), fail more often when two arms act together or the legs carry the robot’s weight than when one hand acts (Figure 27 in Section H.5). However, which stage types fail most differs from suite to suite. When we rank each pair of stage types by their failure rates on all suites but one, the ranking holds in the held-out suite for 55% of the 313 pairs, close to what a random ranking would give. Whether an attempt fails at a stage that it reaches is also predicted better by the identity of the agent than by the stage type (Section H.5). Each category occurs mostly in particular suites and with particular robots, so these rates do not show that the category itself causes the failures.

The most common failure stage of a task is also usually the same in both settings. Of the tasks whose failures have a single most common stage in both settings, 81% have the same such stage in the two settings, compared with 49% if each setting’s failure stages were sampled independently. Excluding the tasks whose most common failure stage is the first stage in both settings, the share is still 57%, compared with 9% for random failure stages (Section H.5). Of the attempts that get past the stage at which the other agents on the same test most often failed, 64% pass the test in the Privileged Setting and 33% in the Standard Setting. Part of this link between getting past the stage and passing follows from the order of the stages, because an attempt that gets past the common stage is already closer to the end of the task.

E.3 Differences between Agents

Tests solved by one agent and by another.

For two agents A and B, the cell in row A and column B of Figure 15 gives the share of the tests that A solves that B also solves. The denominator of row A is the number of tests that A solves. It is given in parentheses after the name of A, and it equals A’s count of solved tests in the Standard column of Figure 7. The diagonal is left empty, because it would always be 100%. The last column gives the share of A’s solved tests that at least one agent above A in Figure 7 also solves. A test breaks the order when some agent solves it and GPT-6 Astra fails it. We count such a test under the highest agent in Figure 7 that solves it, so every agent above this agent fails the test. We use the Standard Setting in the main text because every core task has a Standard test and all agents reach the robot through the same interface there. Each of the five weaker agents solves 11 to 46 Standard tests. A single test therefore changes a share in its row by 2 to 9 percentage points. Among these five agents, the order of Figure 7 does not hold. Gemini 3.8 Flash, for example, solves 2 of the 11 Standard tests that GLM 5.3 Flash solves.

In the Privileged Setting, the order of Figure 7 holds more closely. GPT-6 Astra solves more than 90% of the Privileged tests that Claude Opus 5.5 or Gemini 4 Argon solves (Figure 22), and only 24 of the 327 Privileged tests that some agent solves break the order (Table 3), against 68 of 221 in the Standard Setting. Every agent except GPT-6 Astra solves at most 5 Realtime tests, so we do not draw a Realtime matrix. Of the 20 Realtime tests that some agent solves, 3 break the order: Claude Opus 5.5 solves 2 of them and Gemini 4 Argon 1.

Where the order breaks.

Table 3 counts the tests that break the order by suite. In the Standard Setting, Embodied Safety Exam has the most, 13 of its 50 tests, followed by RoboARC with 11 of 50. In the Privileged Setting, BEHAVIOR-1K has the most, 8 of 71. We checked three of these tests, two of which Figure 23 shows. In the RoboARC blanket test, which all seven other agents failed, Gemini 3.8 Flash computed the corner positions from camera images and depth. It grasped the two far corners with both grippers and folded the blanket in half. It then ran four adjustment programs before the episode ended with success. In an iSpatialGym test, whose goal is given as a picture of the finished scene, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash placed a wrapped food package on a plate. The simulator service ended the episode with success at control step 407 of the 1,900 that the task allows. Gemini 4 Argon opened a jam jar with a dexterous hand in a DexHandExam test, which every other agent failed. These checks cannot show that the agents that failed would fail again. The leaderboard counts one attempt per agent and test. A test that one agent solves and another fails may therefore reflect the variation between runs as well as a difference between the agents.

How the agents fail.

When GPT-6 Astra and another agent both fail a test after meeting different numbers of stages, GPT-6 Astra has usually met more of the task’s stages (Table 19). The kind of failure differs as well (Figure 15). The five weaker agents fail without contact at 9.1% to 18.5% of the contact stages they reach, against 2.7% to 3.7% for the three strongest agents, and the weaker agents’ rate is higher in all 19 suites with at least 20 such stages per group (Section H.5). A lost hold makes up a larger share of GPT-6 Astra’s failures than of any other agent’s, but GPT-6 Astra also reaches more stages that need a hold. Per stage reached that needs a grasp, it loses the hold in 5.6% of cases, against 7.5% for the other seven agents, and the 95% interval of the difference, −0.2-0.2 to 3.6 points, includes zero (Section H.5). In a BEHAVIOR-1K task that all eight agents failed, for example, the three strongest agents each packed three or four foods into a lunch box and failed in three different ways, Kimi 3.1 Pro packed two, and the other four weaker agents none (Figure 29 in Section H.6).

Harness.

The harness also changes the result (Figure 15). We ran GPT-6 Astra in Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5 in Codex, and Gemini 4 Argon in Codex and in Claude Code, with the same tasks, time limits and reasoning effort as in the main evaluation (Appendix G). On the 456 core tests of the Standard Setting, Gemini 4 Argon solves 29% in Codex and 25% in Claude Code, compared with 24% in its own Antigravity CLI. The difference to Codex is significant, and the difference to Claude Code is not. GPT-6 Astra solves 34% in Codex and 22% in Claude Code, and this difference is significant also when only the first episode counts. Claude Opus 5.5 solves 26% in Codex and 25% in Claude Code.
