Part of Gemini 4 Argon’s gap may come from how each harness handles a reply that Gemini’s content filter blocks: Antigravity CLI ends the session, whereas Codex sends the request again and Claude Code asks the model to continue. Attempts with a blocked reply pass at 5% in Antigravity CLI and at about the rate of unblocked attempts in Claude Code.

Overlap among the three strongest agents.

Figure 24 groups the core tests of each setting by which of the three strongest agents solve them. Sections 3.1 and 3.4 give the totals. Here, an agent solves a test alone when the other two of the three fail it. In the Standard Setting, all three solve 43 tests and none of them solves 239. GPT-6 Astra alone solves 56, Claude Opus 5.5 alone solves 27 and Gemini 4 Argon alone solves 17. In the Privileged Setting, all three solve 139 tests and none of them solves 67. GPT-6 Astra alone solves 69, Claude Opus 5.5 alone solves 13 and Gemini 4 Argon alone solves 3. The Privileged tests that only GPT-6 Astra solves include tasks of precise contact and of arranging several objects. The Standard tests that only Claude Opus 5.5 solves include object transport tasks. In a ManiGuard task, for example, Claude Opus 5.5 closed the hinged lid of a glass jar and carried the jar to the goal, whereas GPT-6 Astra knocked the jar over (Appendix F).

E.4 Control Approaches

A separate coding agent read the logs of 1,489 attempts, sampled at random, and labeled each attempt with the approach that produced its graded answer (Appendix B). Many Privileged tests give the agent a GPU to run the simulator, and their instructions name no training library. Apart from these, only eight tests give the agent a GPU: the GPU versions of the soccer match below and of a table tennis match, in each setting, and two RoboEngineer tests that ask the agent to train a walking policy.

The labels split Code to control into three kinds. Open-loop programs compute the whole motion in advance. Closed-loop programs read the robot’s state or cameras as they run. Parameter searches try many episodes to find a passing motion. In the Privileged Setting, agents use the simulator to compute or search for a motion before they submit it. Most of their programs in this setting are closed-loop, and 114 of the 549 programs search over many episodes. The same agent can use different control approaches for the same task in different settings. On a RoboTwin 2.0 task, GPT-6 Astra scripted a hand-over of the bottles with the simulator’s motion primitives in the Privileged Setting. In the Standard Setting, it sent end-effector commands one at a time and checked the camera images after each command (Appendix F).

In the Standard Setting, Direct control places the model inside the control loop, so the robot waits for the model’s reasoning before each chunk. In the Realtime Setting, the environment keeps running, and most attempts run the control loop in a program. In a badminton match of Embodied Olympics - Match, GPT-6 Astra let a program track the shuttlecock and swing the racket. At each pause, it revised the program from the program’s logs and won 11–4 (Appendix F).

The soccer match has a GPU version and a CPU version. In both soccer versions, each team has two Booster T1 humanoids controlled at the joint level, and the agent’s team plays a team with a learned policy on the same frozen scene, with a limit of four hours. The GPU version gives the agent a GPU with 12 GiB of memory, the mjlab simulator with the rsl_rl reinforcement-learning library and PyTorch, and training copies of the match that run on the GPU. Its instruction lets the agent train a controller or write one, and it gives an example of training a walking policy with rsl_rl. The CPU version has no GPU and no machine-learning framework, and its instruction allows learning code in NumPy or SciPy.

Table 4 counts the attempts of the eight agents on both versions in each setting, and of the four runs of the harness comparison (Appendix G) in the Standard Setting.

In the Standard and Realtime settings, 17 of the 20 attempts with the GPU trained a policy with reinforcement learning, and none of the 20 with only CPUs did. Of these 17, 14 played the match with the trained policy. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, in the Standard Setting, wrote a joint controller by hand instead. With only CPUs, agents wrote walking gaits by hand, for example with inverse kinematics or a capture-point model. Of the 15 attempts whose final reports we read, 10 tuned the gait with CMA-ES, the cross-entropy method, or a grid or random search. One attempt, by GPT-6 Astra in Codex in the Realtime Setting, distilled its hand-written controller into a small network by supervised learning. We do not count it as training with reinforcement learning.

With the GPU, agents scored in 9 of 20 matches and won 4, all with a trained policy. With only CPUs, they scored in 3 of 20 matches and won none. Counting only the attempts in each agent’s own harness, the GPU attempts trained in 13 of 16 cases and won 3 times, and the 16 CPU attempts neither trained nor won. The same models appear in several settings and harnesses, so the attempts are not independent, and we report these counts without a significance test.

Figure 18 shows GPT-6 Astra in Codex on both versions of the soccer match in the Standard Setting. With the GPU, it trained walking and ball-control policies and combined them with hand-written tactics. Its robots walked 690 m, against 693 m for the opponent’s, and it won 10–8. With only CPUs, it wrote a gait by hand and tuned it with differential evolution and CMA-ES. Its robots walked less than half as far as the opponent’s and fell 59 times. The mercy rule ended the match early at 3–13. In this example, the two robots of GPT-6 Astra touched the ball 150 times with the GPU and 54 times with only CPUs. The opponent’s robots touched it 142 and 97 times, respectively. The goal times in the figure come from the referee state that the agent queried after each goal, and the frames come from the replay of each attempt.

In the Privileged Setting, every win reused the opponent’s walking network. With the GPU, 5 of 8 attempts ran reinforcement-learning code and 2 won. With only CPUs, 3 of 8 attempts won. In this setting, the agent can replay the same match in its own simulator. According to their code or final reports, all five winning attempts reused the opponent’s walking network that comes with the simulator, and none used a policy that it had trained.

We decided whether an attempt trained a policy from three signals: calls to a reinforcement-learning library or gradient updates in the agent’s code, the GPU memory that the resource monitor recorded, and the attempt’s final report, which another agent read. The three signals agree on every Standard and Realtime attempt with the GPU. The comparison covers one task and one frozen scene. The two versions differ at the same time in the GPU, the library, the training copies of the match and the instruction, so the comparison cannot separate their effects.

Appendix F Example Attempts

This section describes further attempts that illustrate the findings. Every attempt is public, and most can be replayed step by step on the exam’s website.

RoboLab, the white mug in the center of the table (Standard, solved by Gemini 4 Argon).

Gemini 4 Argon located the table and the mug in the point clouds of three calibrated depth cameras and found that the mug, 9 cm across, was wider than the gripper’s largest opening. It therefore grasped the mug’s wall at the rim, with one finger inside the mug, and moved the mug to the center of the table with inverse-kinematics targets sent as joint positions. To let go, it set the mug down and moved the inner finger to the middle of the mug before lifting the gripper. The episode, its only one, succeeded after about half an hour. GPT-6 Astra failed this test.

DexToolBench, red brush (Standard, solved by none of the three strongest agents).

A DexToolBench task asks the agent to move a tool with a dexterous hand through goal poses, 38 in this task. Claude Opus 5.5 pushed the brush until it stuck out over the table edge, grasped it and reached goals 0 to 4. Goal 5 needed a 90-degree turn about the brush’s long axis. The palm-down grasp could not make it, and the brush flew out of the hand as the arm changed configuration.

RoboARC, IKEA Stegesund (Privileged, failed).

With the full state, GPT-6 Astra pressed the halves together, slid in the shelf and drove the first bolt. Its hex key turned only 120 degrees per insertion, so one bolt took 40 minutes, and at the three-hour limit the second bolt was still 3.7 mm short. None of the three strongest agents solved this task.

BEHAVIOR-1K, setting a table (Privileged, failed).

GPT-6 Astra spent 62 minutes placing two plates, and the robot then tipped over against the kitchen island on the way to the fridge.

RoboARC, threading a rope through six holes (Standard, failed).

Claude Opus 5.5 mapped the wall, its holes and the coiled rope from depth point clouds. The rope slipped from the gripper whenever the robot turned its wrist, and the agent threaded none of the six holes.

RoboDojo, inserting a key (Standard, failed).

Claude Opus 5.5 located the key and the lock from depth images but dropped the key at least nine times during hand-overs and large joint moves. Its most accurate insertion, at minute 36, was about 9 mm off and hit the face of the lock.

RoboDynamicExam, toss, recatch and deliver (Standard, failed).

In this task, unlike that of Figure 14, the robot catches a thrown ball in a cup, tosses it up out of the cup itself, catches it again and releases it into a moving box. GPT-6 Astra caught the ball using depth images, but its first episodes ended early (one ended when the cup grazed a moving box) and used up its three allowed resets. In the last episode it caught and tossed the ball, but on the second catch the ball’s contact with the tilted cup was flagged as a limit violation.

RoboPaint, a character in running script (Standard, failed).

With no resets available, GPT-6 Astra calibrated the stroke width on a practice sheet, wrote five strokes and then retouched the character in one long stroke for 38 minutes. The overlap and edge scores met their thresholds, but the long stroke raised the total length of the inked path to 2,048 mm, above the limit of 1,450 mm. In addition, one of the nine regions was only 65.7% covered, below the required 80%.

HumanoidBench, opening a door (Standard, failed).

Claude Opus 5.5 kept the humanoid standing with ankle feedback and located the handle with stereo cameras. It tried more than ten ways of opening the door (pressing, hooking, pushing up and using both hands) and pulled the handle back by up to 26 cm, but the door never opened. The agent used 45 resets in 27 minutes.

Embodied Olympics - Fun, dribble slalom (Privileged solved, Standard failed).

In the Privileged Setting, Gemini 4 Argon saved and restored exact simulator states to try candidate kicks in eight parallel processes and passed all 13 checkpoints of the slalom. In the Standard Setting, it estimated the positions of the robot and the ball from the pixels of a fixed camera, about 9 cm off to the side, and its best episode passed four poles before the 120 minutes ran out.

BiGym 2.0, closing the dishwasher (Privileged, solved).

Gemini 4 Argon read the dishwasher’s code and collision shapes and pushed both racks in. The robot then crouched, hooked the door’s front edge and swung the door shut along an arc. Its answer, a 693-step trajectory, passed on replay.

RoboCasa365, defrosting meat in the microwave (Privileged, solved).

Claude Opus 5.5 used Jacobian inverse kinematics and closed-loop control of the base to take the box out of the freezer, put it in the microwave, close the door and press start. The agent submitted its answer at minute 46, and the answer passed on replay.

ManiGuard, dusty transfer (Gemini 4 Argon, Privileged, solved).

Working in a copy of the simulator that it kept running, Gemini 4 Argon wiped 18 dust particles from the box and then tilted the tray so that the potato rolled in without being touched. It finished at minute 26, and its answer passed on replay.

RoboPaint, cursive character (Privileged, solved).

GPT-6 Astra read how the brush model draws a stroke, wrote a C++ program that reproduces this model and fitted three strokes with it. The first strokes that the agent executed passed every check, and the agent submitted its answer after four minutes.

BEHAVIOR-1K, bringing in plywood (Privileged solved, Standard failed).

A mobile robot with two arms must carry three plywood sheets from the garden onto the corridor floor. In the Privileged Setting, Claude Opus 5.5 kept a copy of the simulator running, wrote separate scripts for grasping, opening the door and carrying, and tested each stage in this copy, where a fall of the robot required only a reset. Its answer passed after 72 minutes. In the Standard Setting, the same agent picked up two of the sheets, one in each gripper, but then drove the base backwards and sideways with a single command and did not check the camera images while the base moved, until the robot hit a curb and tipped over.

ManiGuard, dusty transfer (GPT-6 Astra, Privileged solved, Standard failed).

The robot must wipe a box clean and then tip a tray so that a potato rolls into the box without being touched. GPT-6 Astra touched or flung the potato in its first three Privileged episodes, then reset and passed with a new wrist angle. In the Standard Setting, the test failed because a finger touched the potato once while the robot regrasped the tray, although the potato later reached the box.

DexToolBench, screwdriver (Standard, failed).

Claude Opus 5.5 estimated the axis of a screwdriver from the point cloud but could not determine how far the handle had rolled about that axis, and it used all 20 resets that this task allows without reaching any of its 76 goal poses.

ManiGuard, closing a jar (Standard, solved by Claude Opus 5.5).

The robot must close the hinged lid of a glass jar and carry the jar to a goal without breaking the task’s safety rules. Claude Opus 5.5 estimated the jar’s shape and the position of the hinge from the depth point cloud, slid the robot’s closed fingers under the lid and swung the lid shut about the hinge. It then lifted the jar by 1 cm to check the grasp before carrying the jar to the goal. GPT-6 Astra knocked the jar over while pushing the lid.

RoboDynamicExam, toss and recatch (Privileged).

Claude Opus 5.5 used the arm’s Jacobian to compute the largest downward acceleration of the point from which the ball is tossed, and it chose its toss and recatch to stay within this limit.

RoboWits, tipping a cube out of a container (Privileged).

Claude Opus 5.5 tried six pour positions to tip the cube out of the container and kept the steadiest.

RoboTwin 2.0, three bottles into a dustbin (Privileged and Standard).

In the Privileged Setting, GPT-6 Astra read the task’s source code, scripted the grasps with the simulator’s motion primitives, handed the bottles from one arm to the other in mid-air and submitted its answer after five minutes. In the Standard Setting, it sent end-effector commands one at a time and checked the camera images after each command. It knocked one bottle over, picked the bottle up again with the other arm and finished about 30 seconds before the time limit.

Embodied Olympics - Match, badminton (Realtime, won).

A program written by GPT-6 Astra ran in the background, located the shuttlecock with two cameras, fitted a drag model to its flight and swung the racket. Whenever play paused, the agent read the program’s logs and revised the program. It won 11–4 against an opponent that picks its shots with a learned policy.

Appendix G Controlled Runs

This section defines the controlled runs of Sections 3.2 and 3.4 (Figures 11(a) and 15).

Baseline.

Every controlled run of Figure 11(a) uses GPT-6 Astra in Codex with the same reasoning effort, time limit and task versions as the leaderboard run of Figure 7, and the baseline is that leaderboard run. Each run covers the default tests of the 456 core tasks, and Table 5 and Figure 11(a) compare the runs on the 391 core tasks that have both a Privileged and a Standard test. Each run changes one or two features of the Standard interface and nothing else. Apart from these features, every task behaves exactly as in the leaderboard run.

Object-state query.

We add two read-only calls to the Standard interface: one lists the objects in the scene, and one returns their state. The state consists of position, orientation, size and bounding box, linear and angular velocity, and the joint positions of the robot and of articulated objects such as doors and drawers. In Embodied Olympics - Match, the state of the opponent and of the ball counts as object state. The calls do not advance the simulation or use up simulated time, and they never return success flags, scores, thresholds or goal regions. The only progress value they return is the paint coverage of the canvas in RoboPaint. We remove the fields that would reveal what the agent is meant to find out itself: goal markers and zones, objects that appear only later in a BEHAVIOR-1K task, hint notes in RoboCasa365, and hazard labels in Embodied Safety Exam.

Unlimited resets with saved states.

The reset budget of every task is raised to 1,000, and the interface gains calls that save the current simulator state under a handle and restore it later. The simulator service still grades the last episode as it runs. Restoring a saved state does not erase a rule violation that has already been recorded. In Embodied Safety Exam, for example, recorded violations remain after a restore.

Both.

This run combines the two features above.

No success signal.

The interface no longer reports that an episode has succeeded. The episode does not end at success, and no success flag, progress or score is returned. The agent ends the episode itself with a finish call, or the episode ends when the time runs out or the task’s own failure rule is triggered. The simulator service checks the success rule on the state at the end of the episode, so a success that was reached and then undone counts as a failure.

Harness comparison.

For Figure 15, we ran GPT-6 Astra in Claude Code, Claude Opus 5.5 in Codex, and Gemini 4 Argon in Codex and in Claude Code, with the same tasks, time limits and reasoning effort as the leaderboard runs. Codex and Claude Code support only their own provider’s API format, so an adapter passes their requests to the other provider and translates the answers back. The adapter also adapts the system prompt and model metadata, so these runs only approximate a native setup. We score every run on the 456 core tests of the Standard Setting, the tests of the Standard leaderboard. Each group of bars in Figure 15 compares a model’s runs on these 456 tests, and we test differences with a paired exact McNemar test.

Further results of the controlled runs.

Table 5 gives the success rates of each run. Without the success signal, the success rate stays within a few points of the baseline.

The agent uses the saved states to retry. With unlimited resets, only 14% of its successes came in the first episode, and 66% came in an episode that started from a saved state. The saved states let the agent return to the moment before a hard stage instead of repeating the whole task. The state query helps most where the scene is hard to measure from cameras, as in iSpatialGym, RoboDojo and BEHAVIOR-1K, and it changes little in Embodied Olympics - Fun and DexHandExam.

Further results of the harness comparison.

Table 6 gives the success rate of each model in each harness, counted by the final result and by first-episode success, that is, success in the first episode before any reset (Section C.2). Gemini 4 Argon does better in Codex than in its own harness (paired exact test, p=0.02p=0.02 for the final result and p<0.05p<0.05 for first-episode success). In Claude Code, the difference is not significant under either count (p=0.61p=0.61 and p=0.20p=0.20). In both harnesses, BEHAVIOR-1K contributes the largest part of its gain. GPT-6 Astra does better in Codex than in Claude Code under both counts (p<0.001p<0.001), and most of this difference is already present in the first episode. For Claude Opus 5.5, the difference is not significant under either count. These runs are reported separately from the leaderboard of Figure 7.

Appendix H Failure Labels

This section describes the stage-level failure labels of Section 3. Section H.1 explains how they were made, Section H.2 gives the taxonomy, and Section H.3 lists the excluded attempts. Section H.4 breaks the failures down by suite, robot body, agent and setting. Section H.5 gives further statistics, in the order of Sections 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4, and the limitations of the labels. Section H.6 describes the case studies of the figures in full, with further examples. The labels are released with the attempts at huggingface.co/datasets/MLL-Lab/efe-failure-analysis.

H.1 Labeling Procedure

Task graph.

For each of 427 core tasks, the labeling agent, GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex, wrote one graph of stages, such as the graph of Figure 6(a) in Section 3, from the task instruction, the verifier’s code and a successful attempt when one exists. A stage is a change in the world that a person would list when describing how to do the task, such as “open the fridge” or “put the first mango in the fridge”. Conditions on how well a stage must be done, such as thresholds, alignment or “without touching X”, belong to that stage’s condition and are not stages of their own. A condition that is already true at the start and must still be true at the end, such as a closed fridge, becomes a stage of its own that is met from the start, so that the progress map shows when an attempt breaks it. Each stage has a stage type, its prerequisite stages, a condition that can be checked on the replay video, and the contact it needs. The contact is a list of pairs of the robot part that touches and how it touches (who ×\times how), one list for each way of doing the stage. The edges of the graph give the order in which the stages must be met for the task to pass; a stage that holds from the start can hold before its prerequisites. The stage types fall into nine categories (Table 7). For example, material stages change the state of a material, such as pouring or cleaning, and body stages move the robot’s own body, such as walking or keeping balance. The 427 graphs have 2,411 stages, 5.6 per task on average.

Progress map.

For each attempt, the labels give the time intervals during which each stage is met, on the timeline of the graded episode’s replay video (Figure 6(b)). The condition of a stage can stop holding after it has been met, so the progress map can go down. Progress is read from the replay video, or from the logs where there is no video; attempts without a submitted trajectory usually have no readable progress. An attempt reaches a stage if it meets the stage’s condition at some moment or if the stage is its failure stage.

Failure stage, phenomena and root causes.

Each failed attempt is assigned at most one failure stage, so that failures can be counted by stage and compared across attempts and agents. A failure stage is located when the labels give one. If an irreversible event occurred, such as a fall or a violation of a task rule that makes the attempt fail, the failure stage is the stage during which the event occurred, unless an earlier stage had already failed permanently. Otherwise, it is the stage with the earliest uncorrected mistake among the stages whose condition was never met. Mistakes that the agent later corrected do not count. The labels also record where the attempt was when it failed: during the stage, between stages, while exploring, before the first stage or at the final success check. Up to two failure phenomena describe what visibly went wrong at the failure stage, and up to two root causes describe why it happened, with a video time or log entry supporting each cause. A time limit, a used-up budget or the agent stopping is never a phenomenon or a cause: the label names what was going wrong when the attempt ended. A root cause is given only when the evidence supports it, and it may stay at the category level “Control” when the subtype cannot be determined, as in 47% of the analyzed failures.

Writer and reviewer.

GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex, at high reasoning effort, wrote every graph and the label files of most attempts from the inputs above, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in Claude Code wrote those of the remaining attempts from the same inputs with the same prompts. Claude Sonnet 5.5 in Claude Code reviewed each file, with up to two rounds of fixes and a final confirmation round. The prompts were frozen before the final labeling. Section 3.5 uses a second set of labels, which give the control approach of a sample of attempts (Appendix B). Agents wrote both sets of labels.

Human oversight.

We defined the taxonomy (Section H.2) and settled it in team meetings before the final labeling, and the agents assign its values to each task and attempt. Earlier versions of the labels were reviewed by hand and in team meetings. Each error we found was written into the prompts as a worked example: the task or attempt, the wrong label, the right label and the rule. Most of the worked examples in the final prompts come from this review, and the rest come from rechecks by agents. The labels used here were then written again with the final prompts.

Core set covered.

The labels cover 6,779 attempts on 857 tests of 427 tasks, with at most one labeled attempt per agent and test.

H.2 Taxonomy

Tables 7, 8, 9 and 10 list the values of the taxonomy. A root cause can also stay at the category level, such as Control (Section H.1). Stage types let us compare stages across tasks. A stage type names the robot action that directly brings about the stage’s change in the world, and the types fall into the nine categories of Table 7. In the task of Figure 6, for example, opening the fridge is a mechanism stage of type open, and putting the tomato in is a relation stage of type put in. The contact of a stage says who touches, such as a gripper, both arms or the mobile base, and how, such as grasping, pushing or supporting the robot’s weight. Failure phenomena describe what visibly went wrong at the failure stage. In the same example, Claude Opus 5.5 fails with a loss of balance, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash fails with a lost hold. Root causes, such as a wrong perception or an unsuitable grasp, describe why a failure happened.

H.3 Excluded Attempts

The eight agents failed 5,272 of their 6,779 labeled attempts. The analyses in Sections 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4 exclude 500 of these failures, in two groups that overlap in 83 attempts. Table 11 counts them by agent and setting. Both groups are failures under the rules of the exam. They are excluded only from the statistics computed from the failure labels.

Filter cutoffs, 161 attempts.

In these attempts the model provider’s content filter stopped the agent’s session, and the attempt ended or submitted nothing. Gemini 4 Argon accounts for 153 of them, Gemini 3.8 Flash for 7, and Qwen3.8 Max for one. Antigravity CLI, the harness of both Gemini models, ends the session after a blocked reply, whereas Codex sends the request again and Claude Code asks the model to continue (Section E.3). In 37 of the 161 attempts, the labels also give a failure stage with a physical phenomenon, and the column “with failure stage” of Table 11 counts them. Of these 37, 34 are Gemini 4 Argon’s, 22 of them in the Standard Setting. Because almost all of them are Gemini 4 Argon’s, its failure profile in Figure 15 and Table 19 is the statistic that this choice affects most.

Missing trajectories, 422 attempts.

In the Privileged Setting the agent’s answer is a recorded trajectory that the verifier replays or, in Embodied Olympics - Match, a program that the verifier runs. In these attempts the agent never submitted an answer, and the verifier recorded neither a trajectory nor a replay. We exclude these attempts because they leave no submitted trajectory or graded replay to label. Apart from the 83 that are also filter cutoffs, a missing trajectory is the agent’s own failure. Gemini 4 Argon has 134 such attempts, of which 79 are also filter cutoffs. Gemini 3.8 Flash has 97, Qwen3.8 Max 94, Kimi 3.1 Pro 49 and GLM 5.3 Flash 41. For Gemini 3.8 Flash and Qwen3.8 Max they are about a third of all Privileged failures, 97 of 291 and 94 of 311.

Failures without readable progress, 101 attempts.

Besides the 500 failures above, the stage-level statistics, namely the failure rates of stages and the predictions of the failure stage, exclude 101 failed attempts whose labels give no stage progress, because neither the video nor the log shows when the stages held. These statistics therefore use 6,178 attempts, passed and failed: the 6,779 labeled attempts without the 500 excluded failures and these 101. The 101 attempts remain in the statistics that do not need stage progress, such as the failure profiles of Table 19. The 72 of them with a located failure stage, that is, a failure stage that the labels give, also remain in the concentration of failure stages and in the common failure stage.

H.4 Failures by Suite, Robot Body, Agent and Setting

Figures 25 and 26 break the 4,772 analyzed failures down by suite, robot body, agent and setting. Each row splits the group’s failures among the labels in four blocks, so its values are shares of the failures and should not be read as failure rates. The first block says how far the failed attempt got. Failures on tasks with a single stage form their own column. For longer tasks, the block uses the attempt’s peak progress, the largest share of the task’s stages met at one moment, counting stages already met at the start. Its columns are no stage, more than none but under half, at least half but not all, all stages, and not readable. Peak progress is not readable when the status of at least one stage could not be read, and this column holds 448 failures, among them 98 of the 101 failures without any readable progress (Section H.3). The second block gives the category of the failure stage. The third and fourth blocks give the failure phenomena and the root causes. A failure can have up to two of each, so these two blocks can add up to more than 100%. The rows pool the three settings, except the rows of the settings themselves. The robot body is the kind of body of the task’s robot, as in Table 2.

Shares are rounded, <<1 marks a share above zero but below 1%, and empty cells are zero. Gray labels mark groups with fewer than 20 failures. The phenomena and root causes are those of Tables 9 and 10, and None means that a failure has no label in the block. Other contact pools the four rarer contact phenomena, and Balance or gait pools loss of balance and gait failure. Other covers out of reach, reporting and defects that the taxonomy does not name, such as gaps in a painting or folds left in a cloth. No analyzed failure lies at a safety or information stage or has a task or environment root cause, so these columns are omitted.

By suite.

Figure 25 gives the rows of the suites. The categories of the failure stages differ across suites, and in some suites all failures lie at one kind of stage. Every RoboPaint failure is at a material stage, every Embodied Olympics - Match failure is at a competition stage, and every DexToolBench failure with a located failure stage is at a pose stage. In Embodied Olympics - Match and DexToolBench, every stage of every task is of that category. How far the failed attempts get also differs. In DexToolBench and KinDER, most failed attempts never meet a stage of the task, while in RoboPaint almost every failed attempt meets at least half of the stages. In Embodied Safety Exam and ManiGuard, some failed attempts meet all stages at one moment. In Embodied Safety Exam, most of these attempts have a constraint violation. Failures at the same kind of stage can still differ between suites. In both RoboLab and RoboCasa365, most failures lie at relation stages, but the most common phenomenon of RoboLab failures is a lost hold, and in RoboCasa365 it is a failure to make the contact the stage needs. Among the suites with at least 20 failures, a cognitive root cause is most frequent in Embodied Safety Exam, RoboPaint and iSpatialGym, at 28 to 38% of their failures, compared with under 8% in ten others, such as HumanoidBench, MyoSuite and DexToolBench.

By robot body.

The upper rows of Figure 26 give the robot bodies. Each kind of body comes from a few suites: three quarters of the failures of mobile manipulators are BEHAVIOR-1K’s, and all those of quadrupeds come from MuJoCo Playground. The bodies also differ in their mix of settings. These rows therefore do not isolate the effect of the body. Loss of balance is the most common phenomenon for humanoids, quadrupeds and mobile manipulators. Failure to make contact is the most common for dexterous hands and for the musculoskeletal models of MyoSuite, and most failed attempts with a dexterous hand never meet a stage of the task. For robots with one or two arms, collisions and inaccurate poses are the most common phenomena apart from task-specific defects.

By agent and setting.

The lower rows of Figure 26 give the agents and the settings. For every agent, relation stages hold the largest share of the failures, from 33 to 43%, and the shares of the other categories differ by about five points or less between agents. The agents differ in how far they get and in what goes wrong, as in Section 3.4. The failures of the five weaker agents more often meet no stage of the task, and more often lack the contact that the stage needs. Gemini 4 Argon’s failures more often have the not-attempted label. Between the settings, Realtime failures more often lie at competition and dynamic stages and more often involve a timing error. Privileged failures more often have the not-attempted label. Collisions are more common in Standard failures, and losses of balance are more common in Standard and Realtime failures than in Privileged ones. The settings cover different mixes of tests, so these comparisons do not isolate the effect of the setting.

H.5 Further Statistics

Failure rate of a stage.

The failure rate of a stage is the number of attempts that failed at the stage divided by the number of attempts that reached it. Attempts that never reached the stage are not counted, so the rate measures whether an attempt that gets to the stage fails there. For the rate of a stage type, each stage of that type counts separately, so an attempt that reaches three put-in stages adds three stages. A stage counts as failed when it is the attempt’s failure stage, and as met when its condition held at some moment, even if it already held at the start or stopped holding later. To compare the two settings without mixing suites, we compute the rate within each suite and average over the suites in which attempts reach the stage at least eight times in each setting, weighted by the smaller of the two counts. Tables 12 and 13 give the results.

The Privileged and Standard settings.

The two settings differ in two conditions that matter for Section 3.2. In the Privileged Setting the agent reads the exact pose of every object and can reset the simulator without limit, so it can compute a precise motion from the full state, test it and try again within the time limit before it submits an answer. In the Standard Setting it must estimate poses from camera images and depth, the episode is graded as it runs, and the task limits the number of resets, so a precise stage is attempted on estimates and an error can remain in the graded episode. The comparisons of Section 3.2 concern the stages of a task. They do not concern how the agent controls the robot, which changes with the setting (Section 3.5). We split the stage types into two groups by their definitions in the taxonomy (Table 7). A stage type is precise if it needs a tight fit, a mated or threaded relation, a target pose or path, or contact with a moving object. The 13 precise types are insert, assemble, screw/unscrew, thread/hang, connect, adjust pose, follow path, stabilize, regrasp, throw, strike, catch and dribble. A stage type is coarse if it needs only to reach a region, a container, a grasp or the open or closed state of a mechanism. The 12 coarse types are place, put in, take out, gather, pick up, push, pull, open, close, press, switch on/off and navigate. All other types, such as the material types and the body types other than navigate, are in neither group. Section 3.2, Section E.1 and Table 14 use these groups.

Compared within suites as in Table 12, the failure rate rises from 22% to 56% at precise stages, in 9 suites, and from 22% to 38% at coarse stages, in 25 suites. With suite fixed effects and intervals clustered by task, the precise stages rise by 19 points more than the coarse stages (95% interval 13 to 25). These comparisons use different attempts in the two settings. When the same agent reaches the same stage of a task in both settings, the failure rate rises by 25 points at precise stages and by 15 points at coarse stages, and the difference between the two groups, 10 points, is smaller but significant (95% interval 5 to 16 points). Follow-path stages, most of them waypoints of DexToolBench, make up 38% of the precise stages in this comparison, and their rate rises by 11 points. Without them, the rate at precise stages rises by 33 points, 18 points more than at coarse stages (95% interval 12 to 25). Among the types compared in at least two suites in Table 12, the rates of striking, assembling, adjusting a pose and catching rise by 35 to 41 points in this paired comparison, and those of closing, placing and picking up rise by 3 to 17 points.

The labels cannot show how much of the loss comes from perception and how much from control (see the limitations at the end of this section). The labels also cannot show how much comes from the missing state and how much from the missing resets. The controlled runs of Appendix G separate the two at the level of success rates: on these tests, adding either one alone closes a third to a half of the gap. Joined with the labels, they also separate the two by stage type.

State and resets at precise stages.

We join the controlled runs of GPT-6 Astra to its labeled failures in the Standard Setting, using the results of Appendix G. Of these failures, 256 have a located failure stage. Of them, 91 are at precise stages and 97 at coarse stages, split as above. Of the rest, 36 are at material stages and 32 at other stages. Table 14 gives the share of them that each run solves.

Each run makes one attempt per test, so some failures would turn into successes simply by trying again. The run without the success signal approximates such a second attempt. It is not an exact repeat, since the agent must end the episode itself, and its success rate is within 4 points of the baseline’s (Table 5). It solves 19% of the failures at precise stages and 14% of those at coarse stages.

At precise stages (Table 14), 22 failures are solved by exactly one of the state-query run and the reset run, and the reset run solves 18 of them (exact McNemar test, p=0.004p=0.004).

The logs show how the agent used each feature. Of the 33 precise failures that the resets solve, 31 succeed only after a reset or a restored state. The agent did call the state query in the runs that have it. The run with both solves more of these failures than the run with resets alone (16 failures that only one of the two runs solves, 13 of them by the run with both, p=0.021p=0.021).

Let the recovery of a run be its share of solved failures minus that of the run without the success signal, both on the same failures. On the precise failures that have a Privileged test, the recovery of the run with both features is 53% of the recovery of the Privileged Setting, with a 95% interval from 35% to 70% over failures. The Privileged Setting solves 23 more precise failures than the run with both. Stages that follow a path, thread or assemble account for 15 of these 23 failures. At striking and catching stages, the run with both solves exactly the failures that the Privileged Setting solves.

These comparisons have limits. Precise and coarse failures come from different suites. Most precise failures are in Embodied Olympics - Fun, DexToolBench and RoboARC, and 38 of the 97 coarse failures are in BEHAVIOR-1K. Leaving out any one suite reverses none of the comparisons between runs or between the two groups of stages. The intervals and tests treat the failed tests as independent.

Concentration of failure stages.

The concentration of a test measures how much the agents that failed it agree on the stage at which they failed. We measure it with the Simpson index: for a test that n≥2n\geq 2 agents failed at located stages, with nkn_{k} of them at stage kk, it is D=∑knk​(nk−1)/(n⁡(n−1))D=\sum_{k}n_{k}(n_{k}-1)/\bigl(n(n-1)\bigr), the share of pairs of these agents that failed at the same stage. We average DD over the tests of a setting whose tasks have at least two counted stages, and resample tests 2,000 times for the 95% interval. If each agent’s failure stage is sampled independently with probabilities qkq_{k}, the expected value of DD is ∑kqk2\sum_{k}q_{k}^{2}. The random-stage value, the gray bars of Figure 13, assumes that each agent fails at a random stage but keeps one property of the observed failures: where in a task they usually fall. First, we order the KK stages of each task graph topologically, breaking ties by their order in the task file, so that the ii-th stage covers the interval [(i−1)/K,i/K][(i-1)/K,i/K]. Second, over all failures in the other tasks of the same setting that have at least two stages, we build a ten-bin histogram of the relative position (i−1/2)/K(i-1/2)/K of the failure stage. Third, each stage receives the mass of this histogram over its interval, and these masses are the probabilities qkq_{k}. A simpler uniform baseline, qk=1/Kq_{k}=1/K for a task with KK stages, gives 28% in the Privileged Setting, 28% in the Standard Setting and 30% in the Realtime Setting. This baseline ignores that early stages fail more often, so the main text does not use it. The value of DD for the actual failure stages exceeds the random-stage value in 74% of Standard and 64% of Privileged tests, compared with about 39% in both if the failure stages were sampled from the random-stage probabilities qkq_{k}. The 95% interval of the mean difference is 21 to 28 points in the Standard Setting and 14 to 22 points in the Privileged Setting. In the Realtime Setting, which Section 3.3 excludes because only 27 tests qualify, the concentration is 53%, compared with 43% for random failure stages, and the interval of the difference, 1 to 20 points, lies just above zero. On tasks with at least three stages, the concentration in the Standard Setting is 50% over 194 tests, compared with 26% for random failure stages and 18% for the uniform baseline. The comparison with random failure stages assumes that, apart from where in a task failures usually fall, the failure stages of different agents are independent. Because each agent makes one attempt per test, every pair counted in DD compares two different agents. For the three strongest agents alone, we use the Standard tests that at least two of them failed at located stages, and we build the histogram from their failures on the other tasks. Over these 217 tests, the concentration is 56% (95% interval 50% to 62%), compared with 31% for random failure stages, and the 95% interval of the difference is 20 to 31 points. With the histogram of the eight agents, the random-stage value is 35%. Pairs that agree at a stage after the first contribute 28 points of the 56%, compared with 13 for random failure stages. In 34% of these tests, exactly two of the three agents have located failures, so the concentration on each such test is either 0 or 1. Among the located Standard failures, 62% of those of the five weaker agents are at the first stage, compared with 41% for the three strongest. In the Privileged Setting, 69 tests qualify, and 78% of them have exactly two located failures among these agents. The concentration is 40%, compared with 25% for random failure stages, and the 95% interval of the difference is 5 to 25 points.

Shared failure stages.

We count the Standard tests with at least three stages that four or more agents failed. In 64 of these 190 tests, at least 80% of the failures fall on one stage. Table 15 lists one example per suite among the 64. The Realtime test of the same RoboDynamicExam task as Figure 14 shows the same shared stage: seven agents failed at the recatch.

The common failure stage.

A test has a single most common failure stage when one stage holds more of its located failures than any other. In all, 203 Privileged and 264 Standard tests have one. For the statements of Section 3.3 built on it, the stages of a task are ordered by their depth in the task graph, with ties broken by the order in the task file. To ask whether stage types predict this stage, we estimate, for each setting, how often each stage type fails once an attempt reaches it, using the tasks other than the test’s own. Each rate is shrunk toward the setting’s mean rate with the weight of ten attempts. A second variant uses the rate of each type within the test’s own suite, shrunk toward the pooled rate of the type in the same way. In a sequential model with failure rates h1,…,hKh_{1},\dots,h_{K} in stage order, the chance that the failure stage is stage kk is proportional to hk​∏j<k(1−hj)h_{k}\prod_{j<k}(1-h_{j}). The predicted stage is the one with the highest chance, and the concentration expected under these rates is ∑kqk2\sum_{k}q_{k}^{2} for the normalized chances qkq_{k}. To measure how strongly getting past the common stage predicts passing the test, we take for each attempt the most common failure stage of the other agents’ failed attempts on the same test, when at least two of them failed there and no other stage ties with it. We count the attempt as past this stage when its progress map shows the stage met at some moment. Two agents share a failure phenomenon when their labels name at least one phenomenon in common, and pairs in which either attempt has no phenomenon are excluded. Agents that fail at the same stage need not fail there in the same way: in the Standard Setting, two agents that failed at the same stage share a failure phenomenon in 40% of pairs, as in the RoboDynamicExam task of Figure 14 (Section H.6).

Table 16 compares the common failure stage with what the stage types predict, with rates from the other tasks and with rates from the same suite, and Section 3.3 reports the rates from the other tasks. A prediction from the stage types finds the common stage in 73% of the tests, and always naming the first stage finds it in 65%. On tasks with at least two types of stages, the two rules find it in 67% and 56%. The concentration it predicts is 36% in the Privileged and 48% in the Standard Setting, against 50% and 61% observed. Table 17 shows how strongly getting past the common stage predicts passing the test. Part of this link follows from the order of the stages, since an attempt that reached more stages is closer to the end. The settings still differ: in the Privileged Setting most attempts that pass the common stage go on to pass the test, while in the Standard Setting fewer than half do, and most of the others fail at a later stage.

The common failure stage across settings.

In all, 188 tasks have a single most common failure stage in both the Privileged and the Standard Setting, and it is the same stage in 152 of them, or 81%. For a baseline, we sample, for each of these tasks and each setting, as many failure stages as the task has located failures in that setting. The samples are independent, with the stage probabilities qkPq^{\mathrm{P}}_{k} and qkSq^{\mathrm{S}}_{k} of the random-failure-stage value above and the stages in depth order. We keep the samples in which both settings have a single most common stage. Averaged over the tasks, the two most common stages then agree with probability 49%. In 105 of the 188 tasks the common stage is the first stage in both settings, so much of the agreement comes from tasks that fail at their first stage. On the other 83 tasks the common stage is still the same in 57% (95% interval 46% to 67% over tasks). Under the same baseline, leaving out the samples in which both common stages are the first stage, the average over these 83 tasks is 9%. Where the two common stages differ, the one of the Standard Setting lies earlier in the task in 25 tasks and later in 11. These counts describe where failures fall. They do not show that an agent follows the same plan in the two settings.

Pooled failure rates.

Table 18 gives the rates behind Figure 13, for each setting and for both together: every attempt that reached a stage counts, whatever its suite. The stage categories are pooled over all their stage types, and the rows list the stage types found in at least three suites and reached at least 30 times in the two settings together.

Interpreting the stage rates.

The rates of Figures 13 and 27 show an association between kinds of stages and failure. They cannot be read as causal effects, for three reasons. First, each kind of stage occurs mostly in particular suites and with particular robots: the part that makes contact depends on the robot, so legs and torso belong to legged robots, and most material stages come from RoboPaint and Embodied Safety Exam. Second, stages differ in how much the robot must do in them. A relation stage usually covers grasping, carrying and releasing its object, because the task graphs list picking up as a stage of its own in only 11 of the 229 tasks with relation stages. A rate per stage therefore compares units of different size. Third, the taxonomy records what a stage changes but not how much contact it needs. Explaining the rates by contact therefore requires a judgment of what each kind of stage asks of the robot. Opening a door or a lid fails at 38% of the stages that attempts reach. Closing one fails at 19% when it does not already hold at the start, and at 7% if the doors and fridges that are closed from the start count too. Relation stages fail at 36% of the stages that attempts reach with one hand or gripper, at 52% with two arms and at 65% with the legs or torso. Rates with tool contact can be lower or higher than with direct contact: stages on moving objects fail less often when the robot acts through a cup or a racket, while pose stages fail more often when it moves an object through a tool. The same mode of contact can be easy or hard: stages done by pressing or wiping fail at 8% of the stages that attempts reach when they press on a mechanism, such as a button, and at 69% when they wipe or press on a material. The pose, relation and dynamic categories lie between these extremes, and their order differs between the two settings, so Figure 13, which counts both settings together, does not rank these three reliably.

What predicts the failure stage.

We predict whether an attempt that reaches a stage fails there from the setting plus one other attribute, such as the stage type or the contact. We use five-fold cross-validation over tasks, so that the tasks of the held-out fold are not seen in training, and report the relative drop in log loss compared with the setting alone. The stage type gives 7.4%, contact as who ×\times how 6.9%, the stage category 5.6%, the suite 3.9%, how alone 3.8%, the robot’s body, grouped into eight kinds, 2.8% and who alone 1.8%. The agent gives 13%. With the setting and the suite as the baseline, the stage type adds 8.2%, who ×\times how 7.4%, the category 6.6%, how 5.6% and who 1.6%. To test whether difficulty rankings hold across suites, we hold out one suite at a time, rank each pair of values by their failure rates on the other suites, where each value must be reached at least 20 times, and check the ranking inside the held-out suite, where it must be reached at least 10 times. The rankings agree in 55% of 313 pairs for stage types, 53% of 150 pairs for how, and 66% of 76 pairs for stage categories.

Failure profiles of the agents.

Table 19 gives the share of each agent’s failed attempts in the Standard and Realtime settings with each label. A failed attempt can have two phenomena, so the columns do not sum to 100%. The last two rows compare each agent with GPT-6 Astra on the tests with at least three stages that both failed, with ties excluded. Ties are common. Of the 145 tests that GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 both failed with readable progress, GPT-6 Astra reached more stages on 68 tests, Claude Opus 5.5 on 19, and the two tie on 58. Between the other two strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 reached more stages than Gemini 4 Argon in 51% of the 68 such tests. In the Standard Setting, two of the three strongest agents that failed the same test failed at the same stage in 55% of pairs pooled over tests, and two of the five weaker agents did so in 72%. When they did, that stage came after the first stage in 51% of the 277 such pairs of the strongest agents and in 27% of the 1,700 such pairs of the weaker agents.

The shares of failed attempts depend on how far an agent gets: an agent that reaches more stages that need a hold has more chances to lose one. The two rows “per stage reached” of Table 19 therefore divide by the stages that the attempts reached, using the attempts with readable stage progress. Of the reached stages that need contact, the weaker agents fail without contact at 9.1 to 18.5%, and the strongest agents do so at 2.7 to 3.7%. The pooled difference, 11 percentage points, has a 95% interval from 9 to 13 points over tasks, and the weaker agents’ rate is the higher one in all 19 suites with at least 20 such stages per group. Over the five pairs of GPT-6 Astra with a weaker agent, on the tests that both failed, 9 to 10% of GPT-6 Astra’s failures lack contact, compared with 19 to 25% of the weaker agent’s. Lost holds show a different pattern. They make up more of GPT-6 Astra’s failed attempts than of any other agent’s, but per stage reached that needs a grasp, GPT-6 Astra loses the hold in 5.6% of cases, compared with 7.5% for the other seven agents pooled, and the 95% interval of the difference over tasks is −0.2-0.2 to 3.6 points. Per stage reached, GPT-6 Astra’s observed rate is therefore lower than that of the other agents pooled, although the interval includes zero. Among single agents, only Gemini 4 Argon has a lower rate. Constraint violations, too, make up more of GPT-6 Astra’s failures than of any other agent’s. Per 100 attempts, Qwen3.8 Max has 4.5 and GPT-6 Astra 4.4, so per attempt the two are about equal.

Limitations of the labels.

The labels used here were written and reviewed by agents (Section H.1), and GPT-6.1 Sol, which wrote most of them, is from the same family as GPT-6 Astra. Labels come from the replay video and the logs, without the simulator state, so a wrong estimate and a wrong motion often cannot be distinguished. Perception is named in 4% of Standard failures, and 47% of the analyzed failures have a root cause given at the category level, “Control”. The root-cause layer therefore supports few conclusions, and the analyses of Sections 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4 rest mainly on failure stages, stage types and phenomena. Claude Sonnet 5.5 labeled all Kimi 3.1 Pro attempts and 629 of the analyzed attempts of the other seven agents. The two label writers leave the root cause empty at different rates, so the root-cause shares in Figures 26 and 19 should not be used for comparisons between agents. Each agent makes one attempt per test, so per-agent shares on a few dozen tests have wide uncertainty.

H.6 Case Studies

This section gives in full the attempts behind the examples of Section 3, each with its figure. Times are seconds on the replay video of the graded episode.

Carrying in groceries (Figure 6).

In this BEHAVIOR-1K task a mobile two-armed robot must carry a tomato and a carton of milk from a car into the fridge and then close the car and the fridge. The robot must open the garage door and the fridge before either food can go in, and close the fridge only after both are in, while closing the car does not depend on the other stages. Stage 5, the closed fridge, is met from the start and stops holding when the robot opens the fridge. GPT-6 Astra in the Privileged Setting reaches all six stages and passes. Claude Opus 5.5 in the Standard Setting opens the garage door and the fridge, closes and reopens the fridge twice, puts the tomato in and falls while carrying the milk through the door, so its failure stage is stage 4. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in the Standard Setting lifts the tomato but drops it, so it fails at stage 3, and only the closed fridge is still met.

Installing a fan guard (Figure 28).

In this DexHandExam task a dexterous hand must seat the front guard of a fan on its rear guard and close four clips. The two upper clips need the seated guard, and the two lower clips do not. In the Privileged Setting, Claude Opus 5.5 closed the lower clips, seated the guard at 20 s and closed the upper clips. In the Standard Setting it closed the lower clips in the other order, but it held the guard 36 to 39 degrees off the fan’s axis, whereas seating allows at most 5 degrees. When it pushed the guard on, the fan moved, and the simulator service ended the episode at 24 s. The labels attribute the failure to a wrong estimate of the guard’s pose in the hand. In the same Standard test, GPT-6 Astra seated the guard twice, each time for less than 2 s. As the hand withdrew its fingers, the guard came off with it and reopened a lower clip, and the attempt ended when the guard dropped.

Catching a ball twice (Figure 14).

In this RoboDynamicExam task the robot must catch a thrown ball in a cup, pour it into a slot, catch it again after it rolls down and rebounds off a ramp, then pour it into a moving cart. In the Standard Setting, all eight agents failed, and seven of them caught the thrown ball and failed at the recatch stage. In four attempts, the episode ended because the cup touched the slot or the rebound ramp, which the task forbids. GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Qwen3.8 Max hit them while pouring the ball out or moving the empty cup downstream. The cup of Claude Opus 5.5 was still too high when the ball came off the ramp. Claude Opus 5.5 reported that the ball can be caught for only about 1.3 to 1.6 s after it leaves the cup, while straightening the cup after the pour alone takes about 1.4 s. In the runs of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash the ball never left the tilted cup. GLM 5.3 Flash then carried the ball to the cart, where it stayed in the cup again. Kimi 3.1 Pro did not move the arm, and its episode ended after about 1 s, so it failed at the first catch. In the Privileged Setting, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and Kimi 3.1 Pro completed all three stages, and Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Qwen3.8 Max submitted no answer.

Preparing a lunch box (Figure 29).

In this BEHAVIOR-1K task a mobile two-armed robot must put two apple halves, a sandwich and a cookie from a cutting board, and a tea bottle from the closed fridge, into a lunch box, and leave the fridge closed. The closed fridge is met from the start. All eight agents failed the Standard test. GPT-6 Astra put both apple halves, the cookie and the sandwich into the box by 250 s. Driving to the fridge with empty hands, the robot tipped over at 284 s, and the episode ended with the fall. Gemini 4 Argon packed the same four foods by 85 s, then pulled open a tall dark cabinet that it had mistaken for the fridge, and it had not opened the fridge when the episode ended. The labels name a perception error. Claude Opus 5.5 packed an apple half and the cookie. At 210 s, the sandwich slipped from the gripper and landed behind the box, and placing the sandwich is its failure stage. After packing the second apple half at 242 s, the robot tipped over on its way to the fridge. Kimi 3.1 Pro packed the two apple halves by 292 s, and the robot tipped over at about 380 s as it went for the sandwich. Gemini 3.8 Flash opened and closed the fridge but never lifted an apple half off the board, and Qwen3.8 Max never grasped one in its 845 s episode. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash tipped the robot over within 8 s while exploring the kitchen and packed nothing. No agent passed this task in the Privileged Setting either, where the three strongest agents reached five or six of the seven stages.

Threading a rope through five passages (Section 3.4, Figure 30(a)).

In this RoboARC task two arms with parallel grippers must thread a rope, in order, through a grommet in a wall, a ring, a second grommet, a second ring and a third grommet. Each passage is a stage. In the Standard Setting, Claude Opus 5.5 passed. GPT-6 Astra threaded the first three passages by 100 s. At the second ring, the fingers caught on the rim. At 106 s, the rope slipped out of the gripper, and the time limit ended the episode soon after. Gemini 4 Argon also threaded the first three passages, by about 55 s, but the rope never went through the second ring. Four of the five weaker agents did not get the rope through the first grommet, and two of them never got the hold they needed. GLM 5.3 Flash closed its gripper on the rope at 116 s and again later, and each time lifted the gripper without the rope. Qwen3.8 Max pushed the rope end into the grommet, but at 115 s the gripper on the other side closed without catching it, and the rope slid back. Gemini 3.8 Flash lifted the rope and dropped it at 16 s, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash tried to thread the first grommet in the wrong direction. Kimi 3.1 Pro threaded the first grommet and the first ring by 395 s, and at the second grommet the gripper closed without catching the rope.

Fetching cereal and a bowl (Section 3.4, Figure 30(b)).

In this RoboCasa365 task a one-armed robot on a mobile base must open a cabinet, put a cereal box and a bowl from it on the counter, and close the cabinet. The closed cabinet is met from the start. In the Standard Setting, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 opened the cabinet, put the cereal on the counter and failed at the bowl after holding it. GPT-6 Astra tried to pick up the bowl by its rim from 16 s. At 23 s, the bowl slipped out of the pinch and stayed on the shelf, and later pinches tipped it onto its side. Claude Opus 5.5 lifted the bowl out of the cabinet, and at 30 s, as the arm lowered it, the bowl slipped from the fingers and fell out of reach. Gemini 4 Argon put the cereal on the counter and carried the bowl out of the cabinet but did not put it on the counter, and it left the right door open. Four of the five weaker agents failed without the contact that their failure stage needed. Kimi 3.1 Pro opened the cabinet but never got hold of the cereal box. Gemini 3.8 Flash closed its gripper at the bowl at 2 s and came away empty. GLM 5.3 Flash never got hold of a door handle, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash opened a door but never reached the cereal box. Qwen3.8 Max never opened the cabinet.

Disposing of batteries (Section 3.3, Figure 31).

In this BEHAVIOR-1K task a mobile two-armed robot must put three batteries into the wastebasket of a copy room, one from a cabinet in the copy room and two from a desk in an office along the corridor, and leave the wastebasket on the floor. The task graph has four stages, one for each battery and one for the wastebasket on the floor, which holds from the start. In the Standard Setting, the three strongest agents each put the cabinet battery into the wastebasket and then failed at the second battery, when the robot tipped over. GPT-6 Astra dropped the first battery into the wastebasket at 90 s. At 359 s, as it drove into the office, the base caught the door jamb and the robot tipped onto its side. It righted the robot by 542 s and picked up a second battery at 592 s, and it still held the battery when the episode ended. Claude Opus 5.5 dropped the first battery in at 102 s, and the robot tipped over at 486 s as it turned at the office door. Gemini 4 Argon dropped the first battery in at 23 s and tipped the robot over at 90 s while turning in the office. In both of these runs the simulator service ended the episode because the robot had fallen. Four of the five weaker agents failed at the first battery. Gemini 3.8 Flash never lifted it from the cabinet, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash tipped the robot over while searching for it, and GLM 5.3 Flash lost the robot’s balance while searching. Qwen3.8 Max’s robot also fell. Kimi 3.1 Pro put the cabinet battery into the wastebasket and then searched the office without finding another battery before the episode ended.

Hanging a mug (Section 3.2, Figure 32(a)).

In this RoboTwin 2.0 task a two-armed robot must pick up a mug with the left arm, turn it and put it down in the middle of the table, and then hang it on a rack with the right arm. In the Privileged Setting, GPT-6 Astra put the mug down at 9 s and hung it at 23 s. In the Standard Setting it put the mug down at 4 s and carried it to the rack with the right arm. At 9 s, having reported that the peg was through the handle, it opened the gripper, and the mug slipped off as the gripper withdrew and fell to the table. Two more tries also failed, and the episode ended with the mug not hung. Claude Opus 5.5 passed both the Privileged and the Standard test.

Heading a ball ten times (Section 3.2, Figure 32(b)).

In this Embodied Olympics - Fun task a humanoid robot must head a ball from a ball machine ten times in a row, and each header is a stage. In the Privileged Setting, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 3.8 Flash all made the ten headers. In the Standard Setting the agent sees the ball only in camera images, the task grants 5 resets, and only the last episode counts. There, the graded episodes of the same four agents reached five, four, two and one headers. Claude Opus 5.5 first watched the lob twice while standing still. It then tracked the ball in the venue camera, fitted its flight, and timed a crouch and a push up of the legs to the ball’s arrival. From its third episode on, this approach made the first header every time, and it spent the remaining resets aiming the headers with the waist and ankles. In its graded episode the fifth ball fell past the head and hit the ground at 6.2 s. GPT-6 Astra made its first header in its fourth episode, and its graded episode had reached five headers when the agent’s time ran out. Gemini 4 Argon’s third touch, at 3.6 s, sent the ball sideways. Gemini 3.8 Flash made one header, and in its graded episode the second ball passed the head and hit the ground at 3.1 s.

Appendix I Real-Robot Demonstration

Because the Standard Setting gives the agent only the robot’s sensor readings and its control interface (Section 2.1), an interface of the same kind can connect a coding agent to a physical robot. As a first test, we connected two coding agents to a physical robot arm, and each agent played a buzz wire game for eight trials in a row (Figure 33). This demonstration is not part of the exam, and its results are not included in any success rate in this paper.

Task.

In a buzz wire game, a player guides a metal loop along a bent wire from one end to the other without touching the wire. The loop and the wire belong to one electric circuit, so a contact closes the circuit and turns on a light and a buzzer. In our setup, both ends of the bent wire are fixed to a wooden board, and the robot holds the handle of the loop in its gripper (Figure 33(a)). A contact counts as a failure, as in the buzz wire tasks of RoboARC (Section A.1), in which a simulated Franka Panda arm guides a metal loop along a wire.

Commands and video.

The agent controls the robot with discrete commands. Each command moves the gripper up, down, left or right or rotates it in either direction. In each panel of Figure 33(a), the pad at the lower left highlights the command being executed, and the inset shows a close-up of the light and the buzzer, so a contact is visible in the video.

Agents and trials.

The two agents use GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, the two models with the highest Standard success rates in Figure 7. Each agent ran one sequence of eight trials on the same wire.

Progress score.

Each trial receives a progress score, the percentage of the wire that the loop covers before the trial ends. A score of 100% means that the loop passed along the whole wire without a contact.

Results.

Both agents score higher in the last four trials than in the first four, and GPT-6 Astra scores higher than Claude Opus 5.5 in every trial (Figure 33(b)). Averaged over the first four trials, the progress is 65.0% for GPT-6 Astra and 35.0% for Claude Opus 5.5. Averaged over the last four trials, the progress is 93.8% and 62.5%. GPT-6 Astra scores at least 80% in five of its eight trials, and Claude Opus 5.5 does so in two. GPT-6 Astra starts at 60% and passes along the whole wire in trials 7 and 8. Its progress falls once, from 80% in trial 3 to 60% in trial 4. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 0% in trial 1 and between 40% and 80% in trials 2 to 8, and it does not pass along the whole wire in any trial. Its progress varies more from trial to trial. It rises to 80% in trial 6, falls to 40% in trial 7 and returns to 80% in trial 8. In the trial shown in Figure 33(a), Claude Opus 5.5 touches the wire, and the light in its close-up turns on. The two agents rank in the same order as in the Standard Setting in simulation, where GPT-6 Astra solves 33.6% of the Standard tests and Claude Opus 5.5 solves 25.0% (Figure 7).

Scope.

The demonstration covers one task, one robot and two agents, with one sequence of eight trials per agent. It shows that a coding agent can control a physical robot through an interface of this kind, and that the progress of both agents rose over the eight trials. With one sequence per agent, the demonstration cannot separate this rise from variation between runs. It also does not measure how well success rates in simulation predict results on hardware (Appendix J). A systematic evaluation on physical robots, with a grading program and several runs per agent, remains future work.

Appendix J Limitations

Each result holds for one model in one harness. Each agent also makes a single attempt per test, so the results cannot separate an agent’s ability from the variation between runs. The core set excludes tasks that we judged easy and tasks that GPT-6 Luna solved in a screening run, so its success rates are lower than those of the full exam by an amount that differs between suites. Because GPT-6 Luna belongs to the same family as GPT-6 Astra, the screening may also bias the core set against tasks that this family solves. Many per-suite rates are based on few tests. In a suite with five or six tests, a single test changes the rate by 17 to 20 percentage points, and a single Realtime test changes an agent’s success rate over all Realtime tests by about two points. The stage-level and control-approach labels come from agents. The model that wrote the stage-level labels, GPT-6.1 Sol, belongs to the same family as GPT-6 Astra. This shared family could bias the label-based comparisons between agents. Of the 1,156 tasks, 392 have no reference solution, so we have not shown that each of them can be solved in every setting. Time limits differ between suites, the tasks of Embodied Olympics - Fun run with open network access, and results on tasks adapted from public benchmarks may partly reflect memorization of published solutions (Appendix B). Finally, all results outside Appendix I are in simulation. The demonstration in Appendix I covers one task on a physical robot, so how well the simulation results predict results on hardware remains open.

Appendix K Extended Related Work

This appendix extends the review in Section 4. We first review benchmarks for coding agents and benchmarks for robot learning, and then work that uses language models for robots. We then review recent work that runs general-purpose agents on robots, together with the harnesses and benchmarks built for these agents.

Benchmarks for coding agents.

Language models and the agents built on them are evaluated mostly on digital tasks. These tasks include writing programs from a problem description [15, 58], resolving issues in real repositories [64, 175, 104], completing long software tasks and tasks in a terminal [73, 102], engineering algorithms for hard optimization problems [57], machine learning engineering and research [14, 164, 143], writing efficient GPU kernels [116], cybersecurity [189], and operating websites, desktop applications and other tools [198, 168, 90, 103, 179]. Most of these agents interleave reasoning with tool calls [180] and revise their work from feedback [137]. SWE-agent [174] shows that the interface between the model and the computer affects how often an agent succeeds, and OpenHands [160] provides an open platform for building and evaluating such agents. Other work measures how often agents exploit the tests that grade them [196] and proposes practices for building rigorous agentic benchmarks [203]. The Embodied First Exam keeps each coding agent’s harness unchanged and extends these evaluations to robotics tasks. In its Standard and Realtime settings, the agent must interpret sensor observations and often cannot undo an action, and in the Realtime Setting the environment keeps running while the agent reasons. In every setting, a program that the agent cannot change grades each attempt.

Benchmarks for robot learning.

Most robotics benchmarks focus on visuomotor policy learning and evaluate learned policies, from imitation-learning policies [22, 195] to generalist policies and vision-language-action models [12, 11, 112, 69, 67, 10, 120, 122, 121, 110, 38] trained on large robot datasets [113, 66]. Recent world action models build policies on pretrained video generation models such as Cosmos [109] and predict future observations together with actions [68, 182, 94], extending earlier work that extracts actions from generated videos [25] or learns a joint representation of video and actions [81]. These benchmarks are built on physics simulators, control suites and robot learning frameworks [149, 147, 98, 105, 111, 202, 41, 146, 144, 123, 39]. They cover tabletop and bimanual manipulation [59, 184, 100, 87, 63, 124, 172, 99, 190, 17, 16, 193, 8, 110], household activities [138, 142, 76, 106, 107, 71], humanoid and legged locomotion and whole-body control [132, 3, 194, 187], dexterous and tool manipulation [20, 65, 155], musculoskeletal control [13], physical reasoning and creative problem solving [55, 85], aerial manipulation [162], laboratory automation [74, 79] and safety [119]. Policies trained on real data are also evaluated in simulated counterparts of real setups [82], on real robots at scale [201, 9] and in learned world models [126, 42, 36], which can also generate training data for policies [177, 60]. Most of these benchmarks do not need to restrict what the evaluated system can access, because a learned policy receives only a fixed set of observations. A coding agent can run any program on its computer and could read the simulator’s files, so the exam adds rules about what the agent may access (Section 2.1). The exam adapts 24 of these benchmarks and two others, EmbodiedSWE [134] and ABC Sim [4], and keeps their scenes and success rules, so that coding agents can attempt their tasks under the exam’s rules (Section A.2). Its Standard Setting gives the agent observations of the kind that a learned policy receives, so coding agents and learned policies can be compared with the same observations in future work.

Language models for robot planning and control.

Language models have been used to plan tasks for robots, write robot programs and design training signals. SayCan [1], Inner Monologue [54], ProgPrompt [141], Text2Motion [86] and SayPlan [127] sequence learned or scripted skills into plans, PaLM-E [24] and Gemini Robotics-ER [38, 37] train multimodal models for embodied reasoning, and embodied chain-of-thought reasoning [188] trains a vision-language-action model to reason about plans, sub-tasks, motions and object locations before it acts. AutoRT [2] uses foundation models to propose and assign tasks to a fleet of robots, and SOAR [200] uses them to propose tasks and practice them autonomously. Code as Policies [84], ChatGPT for Robotics [151], Instruct2Act [51] and RoboTool [171] turn instructions into programs that call perception and control primitives, and Code-as-Monitor [197] applies the same idea to failure detection, with a model that writes code to check spatio-temporal constraints during execution. VoxPoser [53], ReKep [52] and MOKA [29] have a model specify value maps, keypoint constraints or keypoints selected from candidates marked on the image, which a planner or an optimizer then turns into motions. Language to Rewards [185], Eureka [95], Text2Reward [169], DrEureka [96] and RDA [75] have a model write and refine reward functions, which a controller or a reinforcement learning algorithm then optimizes. RoboGen [161] and GenSim [156] generate simulated tasks and training data, and Voyager [154] builds a library of code skills in an open-ended game. Most of these systems pair a model with an interface designed for it, such as a set of primitives, a planner or a training pipeline. Primitives and planners contribute the kind of classical engineering that Goldberg [40] argues robotics still needs, because robot data are far scarcer than the internet data used to train vision-language models. The Embodied First Exam builds on this line of work and evaluates unchanged general-purpose coding agents on the whole loop of reading an interface, choosing a control approach, carrying it out and revising it.

Embodied benchmarks for language models.

ALFWorld [139] pairs text-based household tasks with their embodied versions and has become a common testbed for language-model agents [180, 137]. Embodied Agent Interface [78], EmbodiedBench [176] and VisualAgentBench [91] evaluate language models as decision makers in simulated households and other embodied environments, and MineDojo [28] provides open-ended Minecraft tasks for embodied agents. Embodied Agent Interface divides embodied decision making into goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing and transition modeling, and EmbodiedBench evaluates both high-level tasks and low-level navigation and manipulation. In these benchmarks the model chooses from an action space that the benchmark defines, which ranges from high-level skills such as picking up an object to discretized end-effector poses. The exam gives the agent the robot’s control interface, so the agent also decides how its actions are produced.

Agentic robots.

A growing body of recent work runs general-purpose agents on robots, many with GPT-6 Astra [115] or Claude Fable [6] as the model. Recent surveys organize this work by model, data, environment and harness [125] and compare agents that use robots with agents that use computers [19].
