This work differs in two respects: the control approach that the agent uses, and the harness that connects the model to the robot. This paragraph groups the work by the three control approaches of Figure 1, and the next paragraph reviews harnesses.

Direct control. In this approach, the agent observes the scene and outputs each action itself. Several studies use GPT-6 Astra as the policy in this way. They evaluate it on RoboDojo, RoboTwin 2.0 and other benchmarks [191, 199, 130], on memory-dependent manipulation tasks [61], on contact-rich tasks with tactile feedback [163], and with demonstrations and its own interaction history in context [88, 21].

Code to control. In this approach, the agent writes programs that produce the robot’s actions. Several studies give a general-purpose coding agent the robot’s programming interface and add few tools for the task. FAEA [150] runs the unmodified Claude Agent SDK on simulated manipulation benchmarks with access to the simulator state, and Agent as Policy [62] has a general-purpose agent interpret camera images, write programs and send motion commands on real robots. Claude Code (Opus 5) and Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra) write task and motion planning programs that generalize to unseen problem instances [101]. With Claude Fable, a coding agent writes a controller that solves Push-T without demonstrations [167] and writes force-feedback programs for contact-rich tasks [145]. In Anthropic’s Project Fetch, human teams programmed a quadruped robot with and without Claude [31], and Claude Opus 4.7, working without human help, was later about 20 times faster than the fastest human team at all the tasks that the teams had completed [56]. Other systems add procedures that help the agent write better programs. They search over multi-file policy repositories that compose perception, planning and control primitives [27], build libraries of programs from execution feedback [93, 72] or of verified skills from a few demonstrations [108], reuse body descriptions, past experience and skills derived from the agent’s own routines [45], write a shared code library that makes every decision without a model at test time [49], infer a program from a single human demonstration [92], let the agent check and retry primitives within Python cells [140], let the agent develop its tools in simulation before it controls a real robot [48], or have one agent revise, on a real robot, the tools that another agent calls [35]. RAX [50] has a coding agent explore online without hand-designed primitives, given at most a few goal images or demonstrations, and turn the successful action sequences into programs for single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile and humanoid systems, both in simulation and on real robots.

Train a policy. In this approach, the agent trains a policy and then uses it to control the robot. ENPIRE [165] gives coding agents a real-world loop of resetting the scene, running a policy, verifying the outcome and refining the policy. With this loop, frontier coding agents train policies that reach a 99% success rate on dexterous tasks such as organizing a pin box. HARBOR [83] has a team of agents set up simulated environments, design rewards and tune reinforcement learning. The reward design methods above automate one step of this approach.

Most of these studies fix the control approach in advance, and Agent as Policy and ENPIRE let the agent choose between two of the approaches. The exam supports all three approaches and leaves the choice to the agent, so it also measures which approach agents choose (Section 3.5).

Harnesses for agentic robots.

The harness is the program between the model and the robot. Harnesses for robots differ in the action interface they provide, in whether the agent can call learned policies, and in the support they add for tracking state and checking outcomes.

Action interfaces. The success rates of coding agents depend on the level of abstraction of the interface [32]. Show-Harness [18] gives vision-language models a small set of semantic action units, which robot-specific interpreters convert into robot actions, and VIA [47] gives off-the-shelf agents a visual interface with tools to probe pixels and set end-effector targets. HexaShell [34] shares 14 general tools for motion, perception and state across all tasks and robots, because code refined for one benchmark tends to overfit it. OpenRUA [23] gives an unmodified coding agent only terminal access to the robot’s ROS 2 interface, its documentation and basic tools. The uni-robot-agent harness [186] supports further training of open-weight models.

Learned policies as tools. Hi Robot [136] trains a high-level vision-language model that sends language commands to a vision-language-action policy. RoboClaw [80] and Harness VLA [192] let the agent call vision-language-action policies as tools, Recursive Harness Distillation [70] distills a strong agent’s interventions in a vision-language-action policy into a playbook for a lighter agent, and Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 orchestrates the Gemini Robotics 1.5 vision-language-action model [37]. The Physical Agency orchestrator [33] plans subgoals, calls vision-language-action policies and parametrized skills, checks the outcomes and recovers from failures. Yao et al. [181] evaluate GPT-6 Astra on EBench both as the policy and as an agent that can also call a vision-language-action or world action model policy, and compare both with the policies alone.

State tracking and verification. Other harnesses add a persistent representation of the scene and a check of each action’s outcome [157], calibrated 3D measurements and a preview of each motion [153], sub-agents for perception, verification and memory [30], or a vision-language model that monitors a policy and corrects it after a confirmed failure [77].

The Embodied First Exam runs each harness unmodified with the models of its own provider, and through an adapter with other providers’ models (Appendix G), so different harnesses can be compared on the same tasks.

Benchmarks for agentic robots.

Several benchmarks evaluate agents that control robots. CaP-X [32] evaluates coding agents that compose perception and control primitives at several levels of abstraction and finds that their success rates depend on the abstractions that designers provide. RobotWorld [178] evaluates agents on 84 tasks in manipulation, mobile manipulation, locomotion, driving and aerial control with executable success checks. EmbodiedSWE [134] evaluates coding agents on long-horizon dexterous tasks and turns successful agent solutions into demonstrations for training vision-language-action policies. RoboQuest [89] evaluates whether agents explore to find the information a task requires, BiGym 2.0 [194] compares learned policies with programs that coding agents develop on humanoid household tasks, and Xu et al. [170] evaluate whether coding agents avoid an obstacle they are told not to touch and propose obstacle-aware harnesses for route planning and contact. Earlier safety studies jailbreak robots that language models control into harmful actions [128], test whether models recognize undesirable situations in images and text [131], and test whether agents that plan with high-level actions reject hazardous household tasks [183]. In the exam’s Embodied Safety Exam, the agent controls the robot itself, and the verifier decides success from what physically happens in a physics simulation. Of the agentic-robot studies above, many report results on RoboDojo, several on RoboTwin 2.0 and one on KinDER [101]. The exam adapts all three suites. The Embodied First Exam covers 47 robots of nine types, which include humanoids, quadrupeds, dexterous hands, aerial robots and a wheeled car. It also separates what an agent can do with full access to the simulator from what it can do through the robot’s sensors alone.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
